topic_summaries.Trump Administration and US Environmenta:

• The Independent and The Guardian both cover the Supreme Court's climate liability cases, but The Independent anchors its framing in a specific disaster (Colorado wildfire), while The Guardian emphasises the broader corporate legal strategy

• GB News focuses exclusively on Trump's diesel export threats and EU trade tensions, diverging sharply from other outlets by treating the story as an energy economics and geopolitics issue rather than an environmental one
topic_summaries.North Sea Oil, Gas and UK Energy Securit:

• The Guardian and Evening Standard take a more sceptical stance — EDF boss lobbying for new projects and business leaders backing drilling framed as contested or "out of step"
topic_summaries.UK Transport and Clean Air Policy:

• GB News also covers a major road project approval and a car manufacturing milestone, suggesting a broader pro-motoring editorial lean absent from other outlets
topic_summaries.Global Climate Impacts and International:
• The Guardian dominates coverage with a critical, accountability-focused lens — exposing methane leaks from COP31 host Turkey, UK banks financing coal, and governments quietly dropping wildfire plans, while also amplifying Pacific voices and climate summit diplomacy

topic_summaries.El Niño, Polar Vortex and Extreme Weathe:

Full SummaryFormer Australian prime minister Julia Gillard warned that Donald Trump’s anti‑climate stance is making it harder to deliver climate commitments, urging governments not to ignore or postpone climate action as extreme weather intensifies and legal pressure builds ahead of COP31.
Donald Trump’s attitude towards climate change is making progress “more difficult”, former Australian prime minister Julia Gillard has warned, as she says that climate issues can no longer be ignored or postponed.
Ms Gillard spoke to The Independent on the sidelines of a pre-COP climate summit in Nadi, Fiji, where more than 3,000 delegates have gathered for a meeting aiming to turn the dial away from further climate promises and towards delivering on commitments made at previous meetings.
But growing domestic pressures and heavy lobbying by the White House for countries to ditch climate commitments in favour of extracting more fossil fuels - led by an American president who has described climate action as a “con job" and “green scam” - is hindering efforts to deliver tangible change.





“Clearly the attitudes from President Trump and others who don't want to talk about climate change does make things more difficult,” said Ms Gillard, who is currently chair of the Wellcome Trust.

How do rain gardens help with water pollution?
 

When a nor’easter recently hit the Eastern Seaboard, it transformed my driveway into a stretch of whitewater rapids and nearly obliterated my perennials, their shapes irretrievably distorted by high winds and heavy rain. Unfortunately, it’s not the first time.
And it won’t be the last: Scientists predict an increase in extreme weather events, including storms and floods, fed in part by human-caused climate change. 
I swept, then hosed, the debris off the blacktop, and used twine to wrangle my mums and catmints back into shape, at least until cold weather does them in. But my experiences and scientists' predictions have got me planning a rain garden.





 What exactly is a rain garden? 
Simply put, a rain garden is a depressed bed planted with native perennials and shrubs selected for their high-water tolerance. It’s strategically situated in a spot where water — from downspouts, driveways, compacted soil and other sources of runoff — flows downward toward it. That runoff waters the plants and filters pollutants as the soil absorbs it. And it means the excess water, as well as the road sediment, debris, pet waste pathogens, fertilizers and chemicals it picks up along the way, is kept out of storm drains, watersheds and wetlands.

How many Amazon communities received solar systems from Saude e Alegria?
 

What impact did solar power have on Ana's health clinic operations?
 

 For the riverine community of Nova Sociedade, deep inside a protected area of Brazil's Amazon rainforest, the Arapiuns River is the only route to the outside world.
The Arapiuns flows into the Tapajos, one of the Amazon River’s major tributaries, across waterways so vast that navigating them can feel like crossing the open sea. Yet during a historic drought in 2024, Nova Sociedade’s residents had to walk as far as 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) in search of water.
“At daybreak, our struggle would begin,” said Tiago Silva, an Arapium Indigenous community leader in Nova Sociedade. “Children carrying water, elderly people carrying water. We all suffered.”





Two years later, the community is better prepared for this year’s El Niño, the naturally occurring climate phenomenon that raises global temperatures and can worsen drought in the Amazon.
In June, Nova Sociedade installed solar panels to power water pumps that fill storage tanks and provide clean water to all 36 families in the village. The Amazon-based nonprofit Saude e Alegria provided the system and has equipped 29 other communities with similar technology ahead of another possible severe drought.

Veteran conservative lawyer quits Trump’s interior department and warns of ‘assault on the rule of law’


John Murdock had been working for the agency for 18 years and his resignation comes during an exodus of longtime federal workers and scientists 




An 18-year veteran of the US Department of Interior has resigned in protest from the sprawling federal agency, denouncing “a deeply troubling assault on the rule of the law” that took place at the department under Donald Trump.
John Murdock, an attorney and self-described conservative Christian, began working for the agency’s legal office in 2002. In his resignation letter, first sent to his supervisor earlier this year and obtained exclusively by the Guardian and Public Domain, Murdock cites “glaring legal flaws” he witnessed within the agency during the course of the Trump administration, as well as concerns over offshore oil and gas drilling, the aggressive push to expand fossil fuels and the flouting of environmental regulation.

“We are headed in the wrong direction,” wrote Murdock, who officially stepped down on 30 September.
Murdock’s resignation and public comments come amid an exodus of longtime government workers and scientists within federal agencies, including at the interior department, which has lost thousands of employees ever since Elon Musk’s so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) began its controversial efforts to slash government employment last year.


View image in fullscreen
John Murdock. Photograph: John Murdock
“Sadly, I am but one of many civil servants who have departed the government under less than ideal circumstances in recent years. If my story helps others or in some small way assists in preserving the rule of law, I am willing to share it,” Murdock said.
In his resignation letter, Murdock said he grew especially concerned about the actions of a top official at the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, or BOEM, an interior department agency that oversees offshore oil and gas drilling. His decision to resign in protest stemmed, in particular, from an incident that occurred last December, when Matt Giacona, the acting director of BOEM, appeared on stage at a gathering in New Orleans to announce the results of an oil and gas lease sale in the Gulf of Mexico. The lease sale received bids from 30 companies, including BP, Chevron and Shell, totaling more than $370m. During his speech, Giacona extolled the Trump administration’s pro-drilling agenda. He then claimed that the administration was “upholding the highest environmental standards”.

Speaker alongside national leaders at a climate summit in Fiji, the prime minister said the expected nasty summer and the demonstrated impact on Pacific island countries – including low-lying Tuvalu – showed the world could not afford to let the goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C “just slip from our grasp”.

US households pay 62% more for water than they did a decade ago, study finds


For-profit water corporations, federal cuts and climate crisis are ‘supercharging water rate hikes’, study co-author says




US households are paying 62% more for drinking water than they did a decade ago – outpacing inflation, grocery prices and household incomes, according to a new study.
Food & Water Watch, a Washington DC-based non-profit, analyzed 2025 billing data from the 500 largest community water systems in the US, which together serve about 155 million people, or 45% of the country’s population. The analysis compared current rates with data from a similar Food & Water Watch survey conducted in 2015. The study does not include wastewater or storm water charges, which are often billed separately from drinking water service.

In 2025, the average household using 60,000 gallons of water paid $531 for drinking water service, according to the study. However, costs varied widely, with annual bills ranging from $133 at the cheapest system to $1,416 at the most expensive.
Water prices rose 1.6 times faster than overall inflation between 2015 and 2025. Consumer prices increased 39% during that period, compared with a 62% jump in water bills, according to the study. Water costs also rose more than twice as fast as groceries, which increased 30%, and eggs, which rose 28%.
Water bills also rose faster than household incomes, increasing 19% more than the national median household income between 2014 and 2024, the study found.
Mary Grant, Food & Water Watch’s water program director and a co-author of the study, said: “Water bills are increasing much faster than many households can keep up with and these escalating water costs impact every corner of the country. Low-income households are being hit the hardest.
“Corporate water abuses, federal disinvestment and climate change are supercharging water rate hikes across the country.”
The increases were particularly severe in some states. Water bills in New Hampshire jumped 177% over the decade, followed by Oregon at 114% and West Virginia at 95%. In Louisiana, Maryland and West Virginia, water bills grew at roughly twice the rate of state median household incomes, while in New Hampshire water bills increased nearly five times faster.

The study also found a major disparity between publicly owned and for-profit water systems.

articles.raw_rss: As food inflation rises, I'm building a small, sensible buffer at home
articles.raw_content:
Do I feel a bit bonkers writing about prepping in our green and pleasant land? Yes, I do. But I also feel calm and a little smug knowing that there is always, always, something in the cupboard – or under the stairs – for a tasty dinner.



The first rule of stockpiling is that it isn’t panic-buying or hoarding. We don’t need a run on the supermarkets for eggs, bread and toilet roll such as we saw in the early weeks of the pandemic. The goal instead is to build up and maintain a modest store of food in case of emergency. This might be a serious and scary global event, such as a cyber attack or conflict. It might be adverse weather, which some areas of the UK experience every year.



This week, 150 experts wrote to Andy Burnham to warn that Britain does not have a plan for how to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for potential future food shortages that could be caused by climate crisis, geopolitical shocks, or cyber-attacks.





You might also choose to stockpile to offset upcoming food inflation. In May, the British Retail Consortium warned that retailers are facing pressures from rising fuel, fertiliser and commodity prices as well as domestic policies, while the Food and Drink Federation forecast that food inflation could reach as much as 10 per cent by the end of 2026.

A new map has revealed which American rivers need the most attention and protection amid the worsening climate crisis.
Only six percent of these water bodies are currently in good condition and 14 percent need help, con­servationists and scientists said in a September study.
That’s because a century of changes to the landscape and groundwater usage have forced species that live in rivers into a rapid decline.





But by identifying these areas, the researchers say there’s already been progress to protect the rivers. Dams have been identified for removal and land has been prioritized for protection around the rivers’ sources.
“We can now point at a map for the first time and say, these are the rivers most capable of sustaining diversity of aquatic life, and this is what each one needs,” Mary Khoury, a freshwater ecologist at The Nature Conservancy, which led the study, told Science News on Wednesday.






open image in gallery
A new map shows which rivers are resilient and which are vulnerable across the U.S. The rivers are highlighted with colors - blue, purple, brown, yellow and green - that correspond to their level of resiliency as shown in the key on the bottom left of the image (Anderson et al., 2026, PLOS One, CC-BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/))
The four-year-long analysis - which included 5.2 million miles of rivers and streams in the lower 48 - showed that a third were above-average for resilience to manmade climate change. Although these rivers may still require restoration.


These rivers are found along the Pacific Coast, the Northern Rocky Mountains, the Great Lakes areas in Wisconsin and Minnesota, in Northern Maine and in coastal regions along the southeastern U.S. and the Gulf Coast.
Vulnerable or below-average resilience river networks made up 15 percent. These were located in the Southwest deserts, lower New England, the shortgrass prairie east of the Rocky Mountains and the agricultural lands of the Midwestern states.



The rivers and their surrounding areas were rated on how connected the river network is, whether animals can freely travel through them, water quality and the condition of the land near the river, how much water it is, and how much its flows have been altered.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow Chancellor, set out his vision in his first major speech on Monday – as the Tories put the economy at the heart of their Birmingham gathering.

Scrapping the ‘grocery tax’: The extended producer responsibility scheme, which the Tories have dubbed the “grocery tax”, requires supermarkets and food manufacturers to pay a levy on the packaging they use.

Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe after the US withdrew its bombers from the base over new security concerns, the Press Association reports. PA says:
 
The Pentagon confirmed yesterday that aircraft which were being stationed at the Gloucestershire base had been “redeployed to their home stations in the United States”. 
The move follows the arrest of six individuals over the past week in connection with a suspected terror plot targeting the base. 
US officials told the New York Times the redeployment of the bombers, which have been involved in carrying out strikes on Iran, had been ordered after more specific details about threats to the base emerged over the weekend. 
Asked at at lobby briefing this morning whether RAF Fairford was safe, the PM’s spokesperson said: “Yes.” 
He pointed to comments by defence secretary Wes Streeting saying there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”, but he declined to comment further on “foreign nations’ military operations”. 
He added: “I would just point you to the president’s words last week, where he praised our police, defence and security services in relation to RAF Fairford.” 
The five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, arrested near the base on September 27 have since been released on bail. 
A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual UK-Iranian national, arrested on October 1, has also been released on bail.

View image in fullscreen
Suncor Refinery in Commerce City, Colorado on Wednesday, July 26, 2023. Photograph: Hyoung Chang/Denver Post/Getty Images


US supreme court to hear big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuits


Court starts new term hearing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state level




The US supreme court begins its new nine-month term hearing arguments Monday in a high-stakes case in which big oil companies are attempting to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits that seek to hold them accountable for the climate crisis.
In Suncor Energy versus the County Commissioners of Boulder County, local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that climate change has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Canada-based Suncor are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit.

If the supreme court justices side with Boulder or decide that the case is not in their jurisdiction, then it would continue in state court. But if the fossil fuel industry convinces the justices, the decision could apply not only to the Boulder case, but also to dozens of other climate cases brought by state and local governments around the US.
“The hope of the industry side is that this is going to be the death blow,” said Dennis Fan, the founder and director of the Appellate Litigation Clinic at Columbia Law School who wrote an amicus brief in the case. “The industry is going for the home run, they’re going for the grand slam. They’re thinking, ‘if we win this argument, there will never, ever be climate change litigation again.’”
Boulder officials filed a lawsuit in Colorado court in 2018 arguing that Exxon and Suncor concealed and misrepresented to the public what they knew about the damage that burning fossil fuels would do to the climate, and that they should pay for the resulting costs of disasters. Initially, the firms sought to have the case moved to federal court. Then when the Colorado supreme court allowed Boulder’s case to make its way toward trial in state court, Exxon and Suncor appealed that ruling up to the supreme court arguing it should be dismissed on grounds of federal preemption..
Typically, cases must be decided by lower courts before reaching the supreme court, but the justices agreed to hear this case while the state case is ongoing. “That’s an incredibly weird thing to have happen,” Fan said.
The supreme court will consider whether it has proper jurisdiction to hear Boulder’s case right now, and whether federal law preempts Boulder’s case from being heard in state court.

Mixed start for pre-Cop as just two non-Pacific leaders accept Australian invitation to climate summit


Anthony Albanese joins about 4,000 people in Fiji for preparatory meeting for year-ending Cop31 UN climate summit 
 
 




The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it is “important that Pacific voices are heard” after landing in Fiji on Monday to attend his first UN climate summit since becoming prime minister more than four years ago.
Albanese joined about 4,000 people in Nadi for a preparatory meeting for the year-ending Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey while facing criticism from his political opponents at home. Pre-Cop meetings are usually small and bureaucratic affairs, but this meeting has a double purpose: it is being held in the Pacific after Australia and regional leaders argued it would help bring global attention to the plight of countries most at risk from the climate crisis.

 
 


In achieving the latter goal, the meeting has been a mixed success. The Australian government invited national leaders to visit the low-lying atoll nation of Tuvalu, but distance, geopolitical ruptures and the expectation that leaders would prioritise a trip to the Turkish Mediterranean resort city of Antalya for more significant climate talks in a matter of weeks made that a difficult sell.
After declining to comment for days, the Australian government acknowledged on Monday that only 14 national leaders would make the trip to Tuvalu on Tuesday, and just two of those – Timor-Leste’s José Ramos-Horta and Mauritius’ Navin Ramgoolam – have travelled from beyond the Pacific.







Australia and Turkey criticised for hosting UN climate conference while embracing coal

Read more
The climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said they would be joined by EU climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra; the heads of the Asian Development Bank and the Green Climate Fund; UN climate chief, Simon Stiell; the incoming Cop president, Turkey’s Murat Kurum; and international journalists.
Australian opposition energy and emissions reduction spokesperson, Dan Tehan, said the number of leaders attending showed the Fiji conference was a waste of taxpayers’ money, a “farce” and Bowen’s “vanity project”.


Albanese said it would be an important meeting leading up to the Cop31 summit. “It is important that Pacific voices are heard, because the Pacific is the frontline of action on climate change,” he said. “For many of the nations represented by leaders here it is literally a threat to their very existence, which is why the world must act.”

 The UK’s G20 presidency will push Andy Burnham to the centre of the global stage. What will he use it for?

Michael Jacobs






This is a chance for the PM to advance his progressive agenda and tackle urgent issues such as AI regulation and climate action





Among the many crucial decisions Andy Burnham has to make over the next few weeks, one has gone almost completely unremarked: what Britain’s priorities will be when it assumes the presidency of the G20 next year.
Burnham has said he wants to concentrate on domestic policy. But with the world in turmoil, chairing the group of the world’s largest economies will be one of his most important responsibilities.

The last time the UK chaired the forum was in 2009, when Gordon Brown presided over the rescue of the global economy after the financial crash. Before the London summit in April 2009, the French president, Nicolas Sarkozy, had wrung his hands, saying that “none of us has a plan”. Barack Obama had a quick response to this: “Gordon has a plan.”


He did. Brown got the G20 to agree to a $5tn fiscal stimulus among its member states, increase International Monetary Fund lending to developing countries and create a new global coordinator for financial regulation, the Financial Stability Board.
But 2009 was a rare year for the G20, in that it actually achieved something. In general, the long communiques issued at its annual leaders’ summits reflect only the lowest-common-denominator agreement on broad principles. The G20 rarely commits its members to doing anything they were not planning to do anyway, and only occasionally makes genuinely collective decisions. One of the most consequential was the suspension of developing countries’ debt during the Covid pandemic in 2020 and the subsequent establishment of a “common framework” for debt treatment.
Indeed, for what is meant to be the effective executive committee of the global economy, the G20 is an oddly weak institution. Its 19 members (plus the EU and the African Union) have no HQ or staff and do not even have a standing website: if you want to know what the G20 has agreed over the past 20 years you need to go to a set of unofficial webpages hosted by some enterprising academics at the University of Toronto.

articles.title: Met Office issues November weather forecast as London braces for 'Godzilla' El Niño and polar vortex impact
articles.raw_rss: Londoners have been told to expect above average temperatures into November as a ‘Godzilla’ El Niño develops
articles.raw_meta: Londoners have been told to expect above average temperatures into November as a ‘Godzilla’ El Niño develops
articles.jina_text:
A new long-range prediction from the Met Office forecasts “above average” temperatures and “changeable” weather patterns throughout late October and early November.




It follows one of the warmest Septembers since records began in 1884.




Experts have said this spike in heat is due to be accompanied by a period of wetter, stormier weather as a result of an unusually-strong “Godzilla” El Niño this year.








Met Office climate spokesman Grahame Madge said: “There are known general teleconnections between El Niño and UK weather in autumn and winter. These can include a stormier autumn and a colder end to winter.”




The winters of 2015 and 2016, which also coincided with a strong El Niño, brought a series of major storms and what experts described as some of the worst flooding on record.




The impact of El Niño




The unusually warm spell precedes what experts have dubbed a “Godzilla” El Niño event, expected to strike the UK through the winter months.




Experts warned the natural climate phenomenon, characterised by a warming of the pacific ocean, could be one of the worst on record, causing a number of adverse weather effects.












A research paper published by the US government's NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory concluded that El Niño "tends to promote the breakdown of the polar vortex, especially in late winter".




The polar vortex is a band of strong westerly winds that circles around the North Pole and traps bitterly cold air near the Arctic - but a weakened or disrupted vortex becomes "wavy" and allows cold air to spill southward into North America and Europe.








This increases the likelihood that the UK will face extremely cold, windy and snowy conditions over the winter months.




Ahead of this extreme weather phenomenon, British Gas has issued advice to its customers on how to prepare, including tips on gathering essential supplies.

Pregnant women and newborn babies are at growing risk of stillbirths, premature births and low birth weight due to rising global temperatures, medics have urgently warned, as record temperatures strike across the world in 2026. 
Three in four medical professionals (73 per cent) have reported an increase in extreme heat causing medical complications for pregnant women, while a similar number (76 per cent) have seen complications in foetal or newborn health, a new survey by the Wellcome Trust has shown. 
Research has linked exposure to heat for pregnant women with higher incidences of early births, low birth rates, stillbirth and other maternal health problems.





“The evidence is very clear that with pregnancy and extreme heat, you get more pre-term babies, stillborn babies, and much more risk of maternal complications,” Julia Gillard, chair of Wellcome and former prime minister of Australia, told The Independent. “Healthcare workers are reporting that they don’t have the tools and training they need to deal with all of this.”
The findings come after the Northern Hemisphere recorded its hottest summer ever in 2026, while the entire world recorded the hottest August on record. Medics and analysts warn too little is being done to address the adverse impacts of rising temperatures on maternal and neonatal care - and have called for upcoming climate conferences in Fiji and Turkey to tackle the issue head-on.

Australia experiences second hottest September on record as El Niño and climate crisis combine


Alpine areas also experience record-breaking heat with snow depth recorded at zero in Kosciuszko national park 
 
 
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast 




Australia had its second hottest September on record last month as global heating and a strengthening El Niño combined to break a string of heat records around the country.
Bureau of Meteorology data showed the minimum night-time temperatures across the continent were also the hottest for any September, on a record that goes back to 1910. Averaged temperatures ranked in the top five warmest Septembers for every state, and the sixth hottest for the Northern Territory.

Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email
Alpine areas also broke temperature records, and in Kosciuszko national park snow depth fell to zero in September for the first time since monitoring started in 1954.
“There’s only one clear driver of this and that’s climate change,” said Dr Linden Ashcroft, a climate scientist at the University of Melbourne.
“This is also a clear example of seasonal creep where winter is ending earlier and spring is starting sooner.”


View image in fullscreen
A map showing temperatures across Australia for September 2026. Illustration: Bureau of Meteorology
Across the continent, average temperatures for September were 2.71C above the long-term 1961 to 1990 average. Minimum temperatures were 2.52C above average for the month, just beating the previous mark of 2.51C set in 2023.


The bureau’s data showed Australia has not experienced a September with below-average mean temperatures since 2004.
Global heating has warmed the continent by more than 1.5C since country-wide records began in 1910.
All states and territories had below average rainfall for September except for Western Australia, which had its second wettest September on record and the wettest September since 1904. In NSW, 45 locations recorded their warmest Septembers on record.

Revealed: the methane mega-leaks from UN climate summit host Turkey


Exclusive: Cop31 leader calling for global curbs on climate-heating gas has landfills producing some of world’s worst plumes




Two or three nights each week, the smell descends. Residents of villages on the rural outskirts of Istanbul don’t know what the smell is, but they have been plagued by it for years: a smell so bad they have to sleep with their windows closed even during hot summer nights. They know the source, too: the huge Silivri municipal waste dump a few miles away that is belching out stinking gases as food and other organic waste rots.
“The smell is not subtle. It suffocates you,” said Kemalettin Özenç, sitting outside a tea shop in the village of Yolçatı. “It’s worse when the air is still: sometimes families linger until midnight out here. Even when you go inside it’s inescapable.”

These gases are more than a local problem. They include methane, a potent climate-heating gas, pouring out of the site in such vast quantities that the plume is visible from space. Satellite surveillance shows that the Silivri landfill is Turkey’s worst super-emitting waste site.


View image in fullscreen
A methane-capture power station near Seymen waste dump, another Istanbul landfill near Silivri, also run by İstaç. Photograph: Bradley Secker/The Guardian
In fact, its average emission rate of 7.4 tonnes an hour makes it one of the worst identified anywhere in the world by a team of expert researchers at the University of California (UCLA). The planet-warming impact of this single leak is equivalent to 1.5m gas-guzzling SUVs gunning their engines and there are more super-emitting dumps across Turkey. They stretch from İzmir in the west, to Ankara in the centre and Antalya in the south, many with “mind bogglingly large” leaks, the UCLA researchers said.


The revelation that Turkey has some of the world’s worst landfill methane leaks comes at an awkward time: in November, the country will host the next UN global climate summit, Cop31, and has put cutting methane emissions at the top of the action agenda it wants all nations to agree on. Turkey’s first lady, Emine Erdoğan, has been a prominent campaigner for zero waste and methane cuts on the global stage – despite the super-plumes now revealed at home – and the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, said waste management was a priority in a speech he made in June.

British government ‘complacent about food as a national security matter’


Experts say country does not have plan to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for future shortages




Britain does not have a plan for how to feed people in a crisis and is unprepared for potential future food shortages, according to a warning from more than 150 experts delivered to Andy Burnham.
The climate crisis, geopolitical shocks, cyber-attacks and energy outages are among the threats to food chain security, according to the open letter, which claims the government is “complacent about food as a national security matter”.

Academics, business leaders, community groups and food partnerships are urging the new government to treat food as a national security issue and work to make the UK’s food system more resilient, in a era when food supplies “can be weaponised”, they caution.
The signatories warn that the “just-in-time” delivery system built up over recent decades “is not fit for today’s or tomorrow’s challenges”, as little stock is held along the food supply chain and the UK does not have any national food storage. Ministers wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s.


“The food system is exposed to shocks and threats from geopolitics, climate heating, ransomware, energy outages, software malfunction and disinformation,” according to the letter.
The experts go on to warn: “These shocks will fall upon a system that is highly wasteful, import-dependent, environmentally unsustainable, and driven by the pursuit of private profit rather than resilience, with millions of people unable to afford a decent, healthy diet.”
The letter calls on ministers to do the following.
 
 
Establish a new system of local food resilience committees under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004. 
 
Audit the UK’s reliance on a few very large food companies and food imports. 
 
Realign national food production around nutritional needs. 
 
Create national, regional, local and community food storage schemes. 
 
Support the decentralisation of the UK’s food supply. 
The warning comes weeks after the National Audit Office, the public spending watchdog, issued a rebuke to ministers, accusing them of failing to do enough to help households and businesses plan for possible emergencies.


The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future catastrophic events than citizens of several other European countries, while the UK is more reliant on food imports than some of its neighbours.

Climate disasters are increasing the risks of child marriage, teenage pregnancy and violence against girls, a major new global study has found, as floods, droughts and extreme heat disrupt the health and education services they rely on.
The new analysis from charity Plan International – which has been shared exclusively with The Independent – looks at health and climate data from more than 50 countries over the past three decades, alongside a survey of 5,000 girls, in-depth interviews, and focus groups in Bangladesh, Kenya, Peru, Senegal and Zimbabwe.
It found that one in 10 girls said they had personally experienced an unintended pregnancy following a climate-related event, while one third said they had seen an increase in unintended pregnancies in their communities.




One in 10 of the girls surveyed also said they had married before the age of 18 – with 36 per cent reported seeing more girls enter marriage before the age of 18 after climate-related disasters.
“When floods leave people completely destitute, families think about financial hardship and marry off girls at a very young age," said Shahina, 19, from Bangladesh. Participants in the study described girls becoming pregnant from as young as 12 and 13 in Peru, while girls in Zimbabwe noted pregnancy among girls still in primary and early secondary school. 

"For girls, the climate crisis is not a distant threat. It is already disrupting their education and increasing the risks they face when they cannot access health services,” said Reena Ghelani, Plan International CEO.


“Only half of national climate plans mention girls’ or women’s health, and despite the escalating impact of climate shocks on the health systems and services girls rely on, just 0.5% of multilateral climate finance supports health.”
Her comments come as aid groups have also been raising the alarm around the impact of this year’s record-breaking El Nino event on women’s health.

Girls collect artificial flowers from the rubble of a building destroyed by a cyclone in Mozambique (AFP/Getty)
The climate crisis is also resulting in more violence against women and girls, with Plan International’s study finding that more than one-quarter of girls also said they had witnessed an increase in violence against women and girls following climate-related events.


Girls are also more likely to be forced to leave school after climate shocks, with schools widely considered one of the strongest protections against early marriage, pregnancy and violence.

Experts have warned the incoming super El Niño could be one of the most severe on record.

This may allow colder air to drift southwards towards into Europe and North America, potentially bringing blizzard conditions with heavy snow.

The effect also ‘heightens the potential’ for wet weather, stormy conditions and therefore flooding.

Londoners have been warned to prepare for potentially severe weather, such as by keeping emergency food supplies for up to three days.

Met Office forecasters explain that the weakening of the polar vortex associated with El Niño can cause cold north and north easterly winds to outcompete the usual warmer North Atlantic drift which influences the UK climate. 
Dr Will Lang, chief forecaster at the Met Office, said there had been a ‘subtle shift in the odds’ with windier, colder weather in the next few weeks far from certain. 
‘The El Niño event is still developing in the tropical Pacific and already it has surpassed the magnitude of previous events including the one in 2015/16’, Met Office climate spokesperson Grahame Madge said. 
‘Globally, an El Niño event has several impacts, including altering rainfall patterns and increasing global temperature overall.’ 
More broadly, the El Niño event could cause more than 450,000 heat deaths between June 2026 and February 2027, a concerning report has suggested.

articles.jina_text:
The government quietly scrapped plans to prepare the countryside in England for wildfires, it has been revealed. This was despite new data showing fire crews do not have the proper protective gear to tackle them.
This summer has been a potent reminder of the scale of the threat posed by the climate crisis, with the UK experiencing record-breaking wildfires after punishingly hot and dry weather turned large parts of the countryside into a tinderbox.

In the third national climate adaptation programme, published in July 2023, the Conservative government, then headed by Rishi Sunak, said it would run a wildfire risk programme in England from 2023 to 2027 so land management would be adapted for the risk.
However, it has now emerged the programme was never implemented, with the current government stating the commitment “was made by the previous government but was not brought into effect”.



The environmental campaigner and author Guy Shrubsole, who obtained the information via a freedom of information request, said it was “appalling” the government “couldn’t be bothered to pay attention to wildfire risks until jolted into doing so by Britain burning this summer”.
After a wildfire spread across an area including several homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands in August, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, convened an emergency Cobra meeting and issued a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues, criticised as being too little too late.


View image in fullscreen
Homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands were destroyed by wildfires in August. Photograph: Alex Dodd/EPA


“Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel in preparing us for the impacts of the climate crisis,” Shrubsole said.
Alistair Carmichael, a Scottish Liberal Democrat MP and the chair of the Commons environment food and rural affairs committee, said it was alarming that ministers had not prioritised work to adapt land for wildfire risk. “It begs further serious questions about whether this summer’s wildfires could have looked different with more resources on the ground,” he added.
Shrubsole said the government must agree a plan to re-wet the UK’s peat bogs, restore lost ponds in farmers’ fields, and stop grouse moor owners setting fire to moorland.
New data obtained by the Country Land and Business Association has also revealed that more than half of the 29 fire services that responded to requests for information had no wildfire personal protective equipment (PPE).
They included the Suffolk fire and rescue service, which had to deal with an “apocalyptic” wildfire earlier this summer that burned close to the Sizewell B nuclear power station and destroyed vast areas of a protected nature reserve.
Standard particle-filtering respirators do not protect against dangerous gases such as carbon monoxide, which are heavily present in wildfire smoke.
Standard PPE can also be too hot and heavy for wildfire conditions. This can cause crews to overheat, or remove their PPE altogether

articles.title: Trust warns of 'tangible' climate threat to heritage sites
articles.raw_rss: A National Trust manager says recent summers have "brought home" the impact of climate change.
articles.raw_meta: A National Trust manager says recent summers have "brought home" the impact of climate change.
articles.jina_text:
Protecting all heritage sites from the impact of climate change "just may not be possible," according to a National Trust manager.
Justin Scully, manager of Fountains Abbey and Studley Royal, said extreme heat, heavy rainfall and wildfire risk were already affecting gardens, moorland and historic structures.
He said heavy rain could overwhelm drainage systems and penetrate walls, causing damp and erosion, while repeated cycles of wetting, drying, freezing and thawing could harm stonework.
Flooding could also undermine foundations, while hotter, dry conditions could increase the risk of subsidence and wildfires.
Scully said the organisation may have to accept it cannot save everything as it is today.
"These last two summers have really brought this home to ourselves and to our visitors," he said.
"Climate change isn't a thing that's happening out there to other people, it's actually impacting ourselves and the places we love. The threat is tangible."
The National Trust is planning for more extreme weather by looking at what could happen to the properties and landscapes it manages over the next 40 years.














"We've got to think about what could be the worst possible outcome and then work backwards from that," Scully said.
At Fountains Abbey, this could include increasing drainage capacity and gutters to cope with heavier rainfall.
It could also result in changing the appearance of the gardens.
Scully said the trust needed to be "more open to how we would adapt," with gardens potentially becoming "less manicured".
"People expect things to look perfect and crisp," he said.

Getty Images
Coastal areas like Ravenscar are difficult to protect from climate change
The trust looks after properties including Beningbrough Hall, Nunnington Hall and Treasurer's House in York, as well as miles of coastline from Loftus to Filey.
It said coastal sites were among those facing the greatest climate pressures, including erosion and rising sea levels.





A National Trust spokesperson said: "Climate change is affecting many of the places we care for, and our conservation work has to evolve with it."
Conservation decisions would consider the significance of a place, the benefit it brings to people and whether an approach is sustainable long term, they added.

National Trust
The water cascade into the Studley Lake ran dry during hot weather in 2025
The National Trust is a charity and receives no guaranteed government money, although it can apply for project grants from public bodies and lottery funds.
Scully said some adaptation processes could be "very expensive".
The trust did not give a figure for those costs, but said it would continue to invest significantly in conservation.
It also called for climate resilience to become a national priority, led by a Cabinet-level minister coordinating preparedness across government and supporting long-term investment.
Scully said people should not despair.

Experts have warned the incoming El Niño, a natural climate phenomenon characterised by the warming of sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, could be one of the worst on record.








A research paper published by the US government's NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory concluded that El Niño "tends to promote the breakdown of the polar vortex, especially in late winter".




The polar vortex is a band of strong westerly winds that circles around the North Pole and traps bitterly cold air near the Arctic - but a weakened or disrupted vortex becomes "wavy" and allows cold air to spill southward into North America and Europe.




That would make the UK likely to face extremely cold, windy and snowy conditions over the coming months.




As fears grow over the weather phenomenon, British Gas has advice on how to to get you and your home ready for heavy snowfall.

It says that emergency kit should include medicines, drinking water, non-perishable food and snacks, and extra blankets. 




Other advice includes improving home insulation, protecting pipes against freezing, and checking your car’s brakes, heater, tyres and windscreen wipers to see they are in good working order.








It says “if you can keep your fuel tank half full during snowy conditions, all the better.”




It also advises checking in on elderly or vulnerable relatives and neighbours to make sure they’ve got everything they need to get through a cold snap.

Southern California swelters as late-season heatwave smothers region


Temperatures expected to hover around 100F in downtown LA and even hotter inland, raising concerns about wildfires




Southern California faced scorching heatwaves this summer that made locals wonder what happened to their famed Mediterranean climate.
Now, the fall is bringing heatwaves too.

Friday kicked off a new round of long-duration heatwave advisories from the National Weather Service (NWS), which expects unseasonably high temperatures to linger for at least a week. Temperatures are expected to hover near 100F in downtown Los Angeles, and spike well into the triple digits farther inland, raising the risk of both heat-related illness and wildfires.
“We’re expecting temperatures will run some 15-20 degrees above normal – that’s pretty significant,” said Richard Bann, a meteorologist with the NWS’s Weather Prediction Center. “Stay cool. Stay hydrated. Limit exposure to the sun.”







US arrests California man for allegedly smuggling $300m worth of computer servers to China

Read more
October heatwaves are not uncommon in southern California. They’re caused by ridges of high air pressure that park themselves above the region. This year, they’re also influenced by an ongoing marine heatwave that, in turn, is driving a strong El Niño – a year of above-average surface-water temperature in the Pacific Ocean.
But experts say the severity and duration of this year’s fall heatwave is extreme, and likely to become more common in the future as the climate crisis nudges global temperatures higher.
“The extremely hot temperature Friday is rare,” said V Kelly Turner, a professor of geography and urban planning at UCLA. “Nearly 7F hotter than the hottest October 2 ever and about 30 degrees higher than historical averages around 75F.”


If there’s a silver lining for southern California, it’s that current forecasts do not call for strong winds that would threaten to fuel and spread wildfires – though the increased heat and low soil moisture still makes them more likely.
It’s difficult for scientists to point to a specific event and describe it as an effect of climate change, said David Neelin, an atmospheric physicist who researches climate change at UCLA.
But research is showing that with every half-degree of global warming, heatwaves become both more likely and longer lasting.
“Overall, it’s hard to escape that a warmer climate adds to the strength of heatwaves,” Neelin said. “It adds to the probability of heatwaves and the likelihood of getting longer-duration heatwaves.”

Energy UK, the body that represents energy suppliers, has urged Andy Burnham to help households in need and continue to remove levies from bills with the average annual energy bill expected to surge in the winter. 
The organisation said that household bills could rise to £2,100 by January, approaching the cost levels of 2022 when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine forced ministers to intervene in the resulting gas crisis.



 
Burnham has pledged to give households “breathing space, that can take the pressure off”, cutting VAT to the sum of £45 from electricity bills.  
But Energy UK said this will not go far enough, with customer debt projected to reach £7bn by the end of the year. 
Bills increased by 4 per cent on Thursday 1 October, an average of £5 a month for homes on variable energy tarrifs. The average annual bill will now be £1,723 but next year, forecasters predict it will rise by 16 per cent or £276.  
The support measures Burnham shoud enact 
Energy UK wants the Government to deliver targeted support above the current Warm Home Discount in the form of rebates and launch a debt relief scheme for billpayers.



 
In August, it said households in need should receive £450 in rebates a year to effectively address the fuel poverty gap. 
The current discount of £150 a year was recently expanded to six million households, with the scheme being extended to winter 2030/31.  
Dhara Vyas, the chief executive of Energy UK, warned energy bills could reach the levels last seen in 2022 this winter. 
The body has also suggested a debt relief scheme for the most adversely affected and removing further levies from bills and placing them on general taxation.  
Vyas said: “We cannot afford to wait for the same scale of crisis before acting again. We must heed the lessons from that time. 
“The Government must act now to prevent this situation getting worse and causing even more problems over the longer term. Last-minute emergency interventions run the risk of being badly targeted and costing us all more. 
“This immediate action must be followed by more permanent measures to tackle the problems of high energy bills and debt – including their effect on inflation and the wider economy – which we know will persist otherwise.”



 
Middle East crisis causing prices to rise 
The energy crisis in 2022 prompted then prime minister Liz Truss to cap bills at £2500 with the Energy Price Guarantee. 
As energy usage has gone down in recent years, Energy UK said that the £2,500 annual bill would be equivalent to £2,100 by today’s energy levels. 
The steep rise in energy prices follows widespread supply disruption because of the conflict in the Middle East. 
Gas storage levels across Europe have dwindled as a result of the seven-month upheaval to energy supplies.

articles.title: Met Office issues polar vortex update amid London El Nino fears
articles.raw_rss: An unprecedented “Godzilla” El Niño event is set to hit the capital
articles.raw_meta: An unprecedented “Godzilla” El Niño event is set to hit the capital
articles.jina_text:
An unprecedented “Godzilla” El Niño event is set to hit the capital this winter, on the back of a record setting dry and hot summer.








The incoming El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterised by the warming of sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, could be one of the worst on record, according to experts. 




A research paper published by the US government's NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory concluded that El Niño "tends to promote the breakdown of the polar vortex, especially in late winter".




The polar vortex is a band of strong westerly winds that circles around the North Pole and traps bitterly cold air near the Arctic - but a weakened or disrupted vortex becomes "wavy" and allows cold air to spill southward into North America and Europe.




That would make the UK likely to face extremely windy and snowy conditions over the coming months. 


Map of the Pacific Ocean
aapsky - stock.adobe.com




A Met Office spokesperson said: “Through the latter part of the winter, following a peak in El Niño, the stratospheric Polar Vortex can become weaker, leading to an increased chance of Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW) events unfurling, increasing the potential for cold weather.”











SSW, which involves warming between 10km and 50km above the Earth’s surface, can cause cold air to rush downwards, impacting the jet stream and potentially creating a “blocking pattern”.




This could cause cold conditions to stay for the remainder of 2026.




Dr Will Lang, chief forecaster at the Met Office, said it was a “subtle shift in the odds” that El Niño would cause havoc in the coming weeks, rather than a certainty.







He said: “We are going in with a heightened potential for wet weather, heightened potential for potentially stormy conditions, and that leads through to a heightened potential for flooding.”




Grahame Madge, a Met Office climate spokesman, said: “The El Niño event is still developing in the tropical Pacific and already it has surpassed the magnitude of previous events including the one in 2015/16.

“There are known teleconnections between El Niño and the UK autumn and winter period. For example, there is a tendency towards a stormier start to autumn and winter and similarly there is a trend towards colder spells at the end of winter.”

articles.title: Anti-Ulez activist jailed for blowing up camera in ‘terrorism-linked’ explosion
articles.raw_rss: Retired electrical appliances engineer Kevin Rees sparked a major police investigation.
articles.raw_meta: Retired electrical appliances engineer Kevin Rees sparked a major police investigation.
articles.jina_text:
An anti-Ulez activist who blew up a camera enforcing the scheme in London in a terrorism-linked explosion has been jailed for 15 years.




Retired electrical appliances engineer Kevin Rees, 64, sparked a major police investigation when he detonated explosives in the Ulez camera in Willersley Avenue, Sidcup, south London, at about 6.45pm on December 6, 2023.




Credit: Metropolitan Police An anti-Ulez activist who blew up a camera enforcing the scheme in London in a terrorism-linked explosion has been jailed for 15 years.




The improvised explosive device damaged cars and property up to 100 metres away, with shrapnel striking the outside of a child’s bedroom.








Counter-terrorism police were drafted in to investigate the blast, and they identified Rees – a prolific poster of anti-Ulez social media content – as the prime suspect.




Rees was convicted in January after a trial at Woolwich Crown Court of one count of causing an explosion likely to endanger life.

He was sentenced to 15 years in prison on Friday.




The Metropolitan Police said the judge ruled the incident had a “terrorism connection”, which led to a tougher sentence and means Rees will face strict controls upon his release from prison.


Kevin Rees who has been convicted of causing an explosion likely to endanger life (Metropolitan Police/PA)
PA Wire




Detective Chief Superintendent James Derham, who leads local policing in the Bexley area, said: “It was miraculous that nobody was killed or seriously injured in the large explosion caused by Rees.













“He showed a complete disregard for the welfare and safety of the people who live in, or were travelling through, the area at the time of the explosion – all because he was unhappy with the Ulez scheme.




“CCTV from a bus travelling down the road at the time shows how it narrowly missed the blast of debris by seconds.”









The Ulez scheme, which requires drivers to pay a daily charge based on how polluting the emissions from their vehicle are, faced local opposition after it was expanded to cover all of London in 2023.




Cameras are used by Transport for London (TfL) to monitor the cars that enter and exit the zone, triggering fines for motorists who have not paid the daily charge.













During the trial, Rees told the court he “strongly opposed” the Ulez scheme – and London Mayor Lord Sadiq Khan.




“I dislike him, dislike what he has done to London,” the defendant said.


One of three homemade stun guns found at the property of Kevin Rees (Metropolitan Police/PA)
PA Wire

View image in fullscreen
The current strain of bluetongue, which is passed on by midges, was first seen in England in 2023. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian


Worst ever outbreak of bluetongue hits British farms


Climate crisis blamed as virus that originated in Africa spreads to livestock as far north as Aberdeenshire




British farmers are experiencing the worst bluetongue season on record, with the number of cases surpassing the past three years combined.
The viral disease, which affects sheep and cattle among other animals, can cause fevers, ulcers, a swollen head and lameness. The tongue may go blue and even protrude from the mouth. In the most severe cases, the animal can die.

The virus, which is transmitted via biting midges and originated in Africa, has spread to Europe over the past two decades, a development the World Organisation for Animal Health links to climate breakdown. The particular strain of bluetongue currently affecting livestock, serotype 3 (BTV-3), was first found in England in 2023.
Academics have said the transmission is inextricably linked to the temperature of the surrounding environment, with hotter temperatures, caused by the climate crisis, contributing to a rise in cases being recorded farther north.



Bluetongue does not affect people or food safety, but Robyn Munt, the vice-president of the National Farmers’ Union, said farmers were having to keep “constant vigilance” and continually check their livestock for symptoms.
So far in this year’s bluetongue season, which runs from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, Defra has recorded 2,201 cases, 1,103 in September.
Despite being just three months old, the 2026-27 season has already seen more cases than the past three seasons combined.
Defra defines a case as a premises where at least one animal with bluetongue is present, so the total number of animals affected is likely to be higher than the number of reported cases.
Farmers can vaccinate their livestock against the disease but Munt said it had been “really challenging” for them to get hold of the vaccines, as it was a “demand-led process”.
“During a year where livestock businesses, due to the climate impact of drought, have carried a whole load of cost in their business that they might not have been expecting, dealing with vaccinating animals and then potentially having to treat animals with bluetongue is just more labour pressure and stress on a farm business,” she said.


This summer the disease has crossed into Scotland for the first time and has been found as far north as Aberdeenshire.
With temperatures still consistently high enough in many parts of the UK for the virus to develop inside the midges, Tom Cantillon, a senior analyst at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, said this year’s record outbreak was a “harbinger of things to come”.

articles.title: EV drivers love their cars, but some passengers feel sick - this could be why
articles.raw_rss: Research shows there are several reasons people might experience motion sickness in electric vehicles.
articles.raw_meta: Research shows there are several reasons people might experience motion sickness in electric vehicles.
articles.jina_text:
Lola Baird has just asked her boyfriend to pull over. Forty minutes into a journey and she's feeling "overwhelmed" by nausea - and can't stop herself throwing up on the ground next to his car.
Lola, 24, from north London, had never experienced motion sickness until her boyfriend bought an electric vehicle (EV) two years ago. Ever since, she's been feeling "very nauseous" when he takes her on long car journeys.
It's become so severe she's even asked him to change his car.
Lola isn't alone. Other people told BBC News that they or their children notice feeling more car sick when sitting as a passenger in an electric vehicle. But at the same time, many EV drivers say it's not been a concern.
So what could explain these reports of motion sickness?
Dr Irene Di Giulio, senior lecturer in anatomy and biomechanics at King's College London whose research includes motion sickness, says research so far suggests some people experience more severe motion sickness in electric vehicles than in non-electric vehicles.
It's something Dr Nicholas Hac, a neurologist at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago who specialises in dizziness and vertigo, has also heard from some of his patients. "They just notice that they're much more likely or prone to be motion sick" in electric vehicles, he says.
"I've heard about it many, many, many times," he adds, saying about two patients a month specifically reference feeling motion sick in electric vehicles.















Lola Baird
Lola Baird noticed that she felt sick in electric vehicle taxis as well as her boyfriend's car. "I started to put two and two together," she says
But research into any possible link is still in its early stages, and some academics say there isn't sufficient evidence to say anything definitive.
Dr Bill Yates, who has researched motion sickness at the University of Pittsburgh, says the body of research is "pretty sketchy at this point".
"There's some anecdotal information, but not a lot of really serious, extensive studies done yet," he says.
'Wonderful to drive... but my daughter gets unwell'
When Mark Quigg was looking at options for a new car last year, an electric vehicle seemed like the best choice because of the lower running costs. 
Mark, 45, from Lincolnshire, says his shiny new electric vehicle has been "wonderful" to drive - but he quickly noticed that his nine-year-old daughter's motion sickness got much worse in it.
She only used to get motion sick on their 600-mile drives to France during the school holidays, but now he says even the 30-minute trip to the nearest city makes his daughter feel unwell.










On one recent journey, he says his daughter even threw up, which had never happened before.

Mark Quigg
Mark Quigg says electric cars are a "lovely driving experience for me, personally, because they are a lot quieter"

articles.title: Could El Niño mean there are no Atlantic hurricanes this year?
articles.raw_rss: For the first time in three decades there has not been a single Atlantic hurricane in September, normally the most active month.
articles.raw_meta: For the first time in three decades there has not been a single Atlantic hurricane in September, normally the most active month.
articles.jina_text:
For the first time in more than 30 years, a hurricane has not formed in the Atlantic throughout September - normally the most active month for hurricane activity.
With just two months left of the defined hurricane season, there is an increasing possibility that no hurricanes will develop at all. 
This would make the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season the only one in the satellite era without a hurricane.
The biggest reason for this is El Niño, which traditionally stifles activity in the Atlantic but brings a very active season in the eastern North Pacific.
The Atlantic hurricane season was predicted to be quieter than normal as a result of this.
With a very strong El Niño forecast, the US National Hurricane Center in May predicted a total of eight to 14 named storms. Of those, three to six were predicted to become hurricanes, with one to three becoming major hurricanes.
September is typically the most active month for tropical storm and hurricane activity.
But, this year marks the latest date on record since the start of the satellite era (1960s onward) where no hurricane has formed in the North Atlantic.





Image caption, 

While there have been no hurricanes forming in the North Atlantic so far this season, the Eastern North Pacific has been very active with above-average storms




There were, however, four named tropical storms that formed in September: Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna.
All but Edouard stayed out in the open waters of the Atlantic.
The National Hurricane Center suggests there is no sign of any tropical storm activity or hurricane over the next week at least.
Forecasters at Colorado State University, who also monitor activity, suggest the strong El Niño is likely to disrupt wind patterns across the Atlantic and "likely result in below-normal activity" over the next two-weeks.
As the typical peak of the season has passed and is now on a downward trend until 30 November, a season without a single hurricane is looking increasingly possible.
In the historical Atlantic hurricane database, there has not been a year without a hurricane recorded since 1914. However, this was pre-satellite monitoring so it is impossible to say with certainty that none formed.








How does El Niño affect tropical development?




While El Niño is the natural warming of the tropical Pacific, it can disrupt weather patterns around the globe.
As wind patterns shift during an El Niño, upper winds over the Atlantic increase and this leads to more wind shear, where wind changes rapidly with height.
Strong winds blowing at different speeds and directions at higher altitudes rip apart thunderstorms, preventing them from growing into tropical storms or hurricanes.
Meanwhile, the Pacific typically becomes more active during El Niño because the sea surface temperatures here are much higher, combined with more favourable wind patterns.
The warmer waters give storms more energy to grow into tropical storms and hurricanes.

‘We want action’: Fijian climate activist sends message ahead of UN talks in Pacific 


Lavenia Naivalu has seen the impact of the climate crisis first-hand and is determined to amplify Pacific voices at this year’s pre-Cop summit in Fiji






From her wooden veranda in Fiji’s remote Yasawa islands, climate activist Lavenia Naivalu remembers when the reefs were once so healthy, her grandfather would walk to the shoreline and return with fish. But life there has changed.
“The reefs that the older generation of men spearfished in, no longer provide what they once did,” the 44-year-old says. “Young people … now must travel further out to sea to find fish for their families.”

As she looks out at a white sandy beach, eaten away by rising sea levels, Naivalu recounts watching painfully as her three children “feel the brunt of changes in the climate.
“I ask myself ‘what did they do wrong?’”


View image in fullscreen
Lavenia Naivalu’s home on Nacula in the Yasawa islands is on the frontline of the climate crisis. Photograph: Sera Sefeti
The question is personal, but it’s also part of what drives her pursuit of climate justice for Pacific people, whose way of life is being threatened as the planet warms.


At this year’s UN climate talks, known as Cop31, the region will be in the spotlight like never before. Next week, Fiji will host leaders ahead of the climate summit, where Naivalu hopes to draw attention to Indigenous and Pacific perspectives which she says are often relegated in global negotiations.
The Pacific Islands are disproportionately affected by the climate crisis, despite accounting for just 0.02% of global emissions, according to the United Nations.







As climate crisis threatened her home, Alolita was offered a chance at a new life in Australia

Read more
“One thing that triggers me is when somebody else is speaking on my behalf,” she tells the Guardian. “I want to amplify the voices of my community and the people that I represent directly to all leaders.”
Naivalu, an Indigenous representative participating in the Fiji meeting and the Cop31 summit in Turkey, has been a trailblazing advocate for her people.
She was Fiji’s first female mata ni tikina, or district representative, overseeing seven village chiefs under the traditionally male-dominated governance system. Naivalu was also the first Indigenous representative selected to Fiji’s tourism board.

articles.raw_rss: Julie Burchill: You need a loud voice and sharp elbows to get to the top of the grievances hot-list these days
articles.raw_content:
We no longer have a Green council in the People’s Republic of Brighton and Hove – but it often feels that way. Way back before Zack Polanski was even dreaming of being a nipple-charming, breast-enhancing hypnotist, we had the first Green MP, Caroline Lucas, from 2010 to 2024. She seemed somewhat wacky at the time, wanting “ecocide” to be made a crime at the International Criminal Court, up there with genocide, but now seems to have the gravitas of Baroness Betty Boothroyd in comparison to the strange gang of characters who have succeeded her. 



Much as I love my adopted city, it would be Brighton and Hove which spawned an unwashed monster. We are blessed with a huge student population, most posh and incoming. It’s a weary gag among my friends who live in streets colonised by them that the less “house-proud” the front yard, the more likely a house is to have a “VOTE GREEN” poster in the window at election times. 



A few years back, the University of Sussex announced that it intended to set aside nearly half of its land for “rewilding”. You can see why the students don’t bother clearing up their mess, when their elders opine that the best way to achieve “biodiversity” is by mowing the grass a limited number of times – or not at all. 



The line between being biodiverse and being dangerous has been blurred a good deal in this once-lovely city by the sea, where the Green council “rewilded” miles of pavement, causing several disabled and elderly people to end up in A&E. I

It’s a weary gag among my friends who live in streets colonised by them that the less “house-proud” the front yard, the more likely a house is to have a “VOTE GREEN” poster in the window at election times.  
A few years back, the University of Sussex announced that it intended to set aside nearly half of its land for “rewilding”. You can see why the students don’t bother clearing up their mess, when their elders opine that the best way to achieve “biodiversity” is by mowing the grass a limited number of times – or not at all. 



 
The line between being biodiverse and being dangerous has been blurred a good deal in this once-lovely city by the sea, where the Green council “rewilded” miles of pavement, causing several disabled and elderly people to end up in A&E. It was a relief when Labour got the council back (can’t believe I wrote that), but after four years, “rewilding” had caused lasting damage to pavements and even more damage to the confidence of disabled people who found it difficult to negotiate this shambles.  
In 2024, Labour councillor Tim Rowkins, chair of the environment committee, said the council was spending £50,000 a month on repairs to pavements, with a backlog of repairs totalling £60m, and weeds being the main cause of damage: “Parts of the city are completely wild and many of our residents – wheelchair users, parents and carers with buggies, those with visual or mobility impairments – simply can’t travel the distance of their own street safely.”  
Luckily, as I am blessed with an uxorious husband and a chorus line of female fans, this has never bothered me personally – but not every paraplegic is as pampered as I am and many must find their way around on their own.  
After taking over Brighton and Hove, Labour council leader Bella Sankey said the weeds situation was giving her “sleepless nights”.



 
“During certain months of the year many pavements are not accessible for wheelchair users, parents and carers with buggies and those with visual or mobility impairments… as well as multiple resident injuries, our manual weeders have also had injuries and are now only able to weed for a maximum of three hours a day given the physical risk.”

Britain’s electric car market has just had its busiest month yet, with almost 100,000 new EVs registered in September 2026. 
The new figures, which show the Chinese-made Jaecoo 7 was the best-selling new car in September, were announced as the average price of a litre of diesel in the UK passed £2 for the first time on Friday.
A total of 99,199 all-electric cars were registered last month - up 36.3 per cent on September last year. That gave EVs a 28.3 per cent of the market – more than one in four new cars, and five percentage points ahead of a year earlier. By contrast, diesel cars now account for just 4 per cent of the market.





More choice, manufacturer discounts and the government’s Electric Car Grant helped convert EV buyers, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT).
The Jaecoo 7 took top spot for the second time this year with 10,813 registrations, while Tesla’s Model 3 took second place in the overall new car sales chart. Ford’s Puma was third with 6,958, followed by the Kia Sportage on 6,521 and Tesla’s Model Y on 5,946, putting two Teslas among September’s five biggest sellers.



The Tesla Model 3 secured second place in the September sales chart, with the Tesla Model Y in fifth (Steve Fowler)
The Nissan Qashqai, Vauxhall Corsa, Volkswagen Golf, MG HS and Audi A3 completed the monthly top ten. Just two registrations separated the seventh-placed Corsa from the Golf, with 5,498 and 5,496 respectively.


There’s a different leader when you look at the year so far. The Ford Puma heads the table with 42,926 registrations, giving it a 3,453-car lead over the Jaecoo 7 on 39,473. The Kia Sportage is third with 37,085, ahead of the Nissan Qashqai on 33,082, while the Tesla Model 3 sits ninth with 23,704.
The wider new car market had a busy September, too, with registrations rising 12.1 per cent to 350,518. That made it the strongest September since 2017 and the tenth consecutive month of growth. Private buyers accounted for 149,158 registrations, up 13.9 per cent, while fleets remained the biggest part of the market with 190,988, an increase of 9.6 per cent.

Prof Cecilia Mascolo, who led the study from the University of Cambridge, said: “I come from an area in Italy with very high pollution and I am very aware of its not-talked-about effects.” Continue reading...

articles.jina_text:
Many more of us are using apps to monitor our sleep patterns. A recent survey of 18- to 30-year-olds in the UK found that 37% used sleep apps, while data from 2025 suggested that more than 40% of UK adults used tech to track their sleep.
The researchers looked at data from a commonly used sleep app. For 18 months they collected anonymised data from 32 cities in 12 countries, an average of 98,000 people a night.


As well as tracking sleep, the app also counted how many times people coughed. About half of the people coughed during the night, with 1% coughing more than 10 times. The greatest frequency of coughing was recorded in Milan and around Monza, both cities in north Italy’s Po Valley, one of the most polluted areas in western Europe.







Improved air quality linked to better mental development in toddlers, study finds

Read more
A look at the data for Los Angeles and London shows that people cough more in cold weather and there are more coughs recorded when flu is circulating.
Mascolo said: “The hardest part was understanding if what we were seeing in the cough peaks was really affected by pollution or rather by viruses/flu trends as well as weather.”
Dr Tong Xia, part of the research team and now at Tsinghua University, added: “I thought that adding in the confounding factor of flu season would make the link in the data disappear, but it didn’t.”
High daily particle pollution was consistently associated with increased night-time coughing, but effects could also be seen at lower concentrations, well below the World Health Organization’s (WHO) air pollution guidelines.
Mascolo said: “Even in cities with relatively low levels of air pollution, such as Melbourne and Sydney, we observed positive associations between particle pollution and increased coughing.


“The LA wildfires were the clearest and most severe pollution spike in our study window.” Night-time coughing increased by 13 % during the wildfire smoke, and some people experienced effects that were delayed by several days.
Mascolo and Tong also found increased coughing in the London data around the time of Guy Fawkes fireworks and bonfires: “During the first week of November 2025, when influenza activity remained low, days with PM2.5 [particulate matter of less than 2.5 micrometres in diameter] concentrations exceeding the WHO guideline became more frequent, accompanied by a noticeably higher cough rate than previous months.
“Emission sources, such as firework displays, may have contributed to episodic air pollution and subsequent airway irritation, although source-specific data are needed to substantiate this.”
Rather than stopping action on air pollution once legal limits are met, we should be continuing to reduce air pollution.

May heatwaves, deaths, ruined harvests: study of Europe’s summer paints grim picture for the future


EU Copernicus report shows surface air temperatures from June to August were 2.5C above decadal average




The scorching heat that persistently baked western Europe this summer was the worst on record, a report has found, with more than half the continent seared by “very strong” heat stress that felt hotter than 38C.
Surface air temperatures in western Europe from June to August were 2.5C above the recent decadal average, according to an update from the EU’s Copernicus climate monitoring service on Friday, while milder but still deadly heat across the rest of the continent made the summer Europe’s third hottest on record.

The finding comes as a swelling El Niño of unprecedented strength raises global temperatures and supercharges violent weather from South America to Australia. The natural sea warming pattern, which has broken the temperature record months before its expected peak at the end of the year, is expected to cause almost half a million extra heat-related deaths by February.

In Europe, where El Niño’s effects are felt mostly indirectly – for instance, through higher food prices and inflation – the intense heat experienced this summer is the result of fossil fuel pollution clogging the atmosphere.


The report found at least 60% of western Europe suffered through temperatures above 30C on 17 days this summer. In 2003, a year also marked by ferocious heat, this was observed on 11 days, and in 2025 on just seven. The high heat led to a record-breaking 13 days of “very strong” heat stress across western Europe.
Europe saw an abnormally early start to summer-like weather when a powerful heatwave boggled climate scientists in late May, and high heat continued even through September, the report found. Recurring heatwaves, made hotter and more common by climate breakdown, killed tens of thousands of people across the continent while ruining harvests and shutting power plants.
