articles.jina_text:
States and cities sued the Trump administration on Thursday for repealing rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas.
Twenty-one states, led by New York, are challenging the Environmental Protection Agency’s power plant rule. The Democratic-led coalition also includes Pennsylvania’s governor, the District of Columbia, New York City, Chicago and the city and county of Denver. They argue that “gutting one of the country’s most significant climate protections” will set the nation back decades and worsen the climate crisis.

The EPA announced last month it’s revoking the Biden-era rule, and said it is taking a separate but related step to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.







EPA union sues Trump administration to restore collective bargaining contract

Read more
New York attorney general Letitia James said the federal government is showing “callous disregard” for Americans’ health and the environment, and future generations will pay the price. Power plants that burn fossil fuels are a major source of planet-warming pollution.
“Dismantling these protections is a betrayal of American families, and the stakes are too high to allow this administration to once again put profits over people,” James said in a statement Thursday.
The EPA said Thursday it does not comment on pending litigation. However, it said in announcing the repeal that it would save the industry more than $300bn in costs and help “unleash” American energy. EPA assistant administrator Aaron Szabo said in September that it will allow utilities to “make the best decision for the ratepayers based on cost and cost savings, instead of being required to shut down facilities”.


The coalition is petitioning the US court of appeals for the District of Columbia to review the EPA’s decision and strike down the repeal. It says the EPA unlawfully abandoned the pollution limits without properly considering reasonable alternatives or the enormous health and climate costs of allowing more pollution into the atmosphere. The coalition also told the EPA it intends to sue over the agency’s failure to regulate pollution from many gas-fired power plants.
The suit comes as the supreme court prepares to hear a landmark case in which the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, are suing oil and gas companies to force them to help pay for damage caused by disasters linked to climate change.
The case is part of a wave of climate change litigation around the country and the world with billions of dollars at stake. The high court will hear the case on Monday, the first day of its new term.
The rule change for power plants, first proposed last year, represents a fundamental shift from efforts by Democrats Joe Biden and Barack Obama to address climate change and regulate carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that trap the sun’s heat. Environmental groups say it will come at a cost to Americans’ health

Matt Kean warns climate crisis ‘isn’t someone else’s problem’ as largest coal project in NSW history greenlit


Exclusive: Climate Change Authority chair says planning commission did not account for climate-related economic damage in NSW 
 
 
Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates 
 




A senior Albanese government climate adviser has challenged the state approval of the largest coalmining development in New South Wales’s history, arguing “climate change isn’t someone else’s problem”.
Matt Kean, the chair of the Climate Change Authority and a former NSW treasurer and energy minister, questioned why the state Independent Planning Commission had not weighed the economic cost of climate change caused by burning the coal from the Hunter Valley Operations mine before giving it the green light to run until 2045.

The commission said greenhouse gases from the coal mined near Singleton would contribute to climate change impacts that affected the “people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”, but said those impacts were outweighed by local benefits, including “employment, economic activity, support for local business, ongoing royalties and taxation revenue”.






The green light for the largest coalmine in NSW history is shocking proof that our governance systems are betraying Australians | Georgina Woods

Read more
The decision was applauded by the NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns. In an interview on 2GB radio on Thursday, he said it was “the right decision” and “hugely important” for the state economy. “It props up, and is responsible for, literally thousands of direct and indirect jobs,” he said. “It also produces billions of dollars of royalties for the NSW government.”
Minns did not mention in the interview the development’s projected climate impact. The mine’s owners, Yancoal and Glencore, forecast it could lead to 809m tonnes of carbon dioxide – nearly double Australia’s annual climate pollution – being released into the atmosphere once the coal is exported and burned.
Kean said the commission had acknowledged the project would contribute to climate change, and evidence that found climate-related disasters could cost Australians at least $73bn a year by 2060. But he said it had not estimated the climate-related economic damage in NSW as it weighed the local costs and benefits of the mine expansion.
He pointed to a recent report by the UN Environment Programme that found the world was heading beyond 1.5C in global heating – a goal agreed in the 2015 Paris agreement – and stressed that costs would increase with “every fraction of a degree of warming”

 As Ted Schuur stepped along the edges of Smith Lake, a bubble surfaced from the muck underfoot. And then another.
They're bubbles of methane, a potent heat-trapping gas made from decomposing plants and animals that had once been stuck in Alaska's frigid permafrost. But that frozen ground is thawing because the Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the globe. For thousands of years that frozen ground stored dead plants and animals, but the accelerating thaw is allowing them to decay into methane and carbon dioxide. 
“Once you start leaking this carbon out, there’s so much in the ground that it’s not going to shut off,” said Schuur, an ecologist at Northern Arizona University, calling it one of climate change's scary tipping points. “Essentially every year is setting a permafrost record.”





There’s three times as much carbon still frozen in permafrost than what’s now in the air, but all over the Arctic those heat-trapping gases are escaping into the atmosphere. Their release adds to what's already in the air from humanity's burning coal, oil and natural gas, changing the delicate balance of how a warming world deals with the buildup of heat-trapping carbon, Schuur said.
Permafrost is ground that stays frozen — below 32 degrees Fahrenheit (zero degrees Celsius) — for at least two years and often for centuries and even millennia. That frozen ground — found in Alaska, Canada, Siberia, Antarctica and high mountain elevations elsewhere — has special advantages, trapping decaying matter, keeping it from turning into greenhouse gases and just being firm enough for communities and industries to build their lives upon.

 A wind turbine described by its developer as the world’s tallest now rises 365 meters (1,197 feet) above the sparsely populated landscape of eastern Germany, surpassing the height of the Eiffel Tower.
The colossal turbine has been built at an existing wind farm in Lusatia, southeast of Berlin. Once a major center of lignite mining, the region has increasingly turned to renewable energy in recent years. The prototype reached its full height this week and is due to be inaugurated in mid-November.
Jochen Grossmann, chief executive of Gircon, the Dresden-based engineering company that built the tower, said the structure would harness the stronger, more reliable winds found at greater heights. Conventional wind turbines typically have a hub height — the distance from the ground to the center of the rotor — of well below 200 meters (656 feet).





“At 300 meters, we have such constant and strong wind that we can produce more than twice as much electrical energy as with the same facility at today's heights,” Grossmann said on Thursday. He added that it would also be possible to produce electricity for much more of the year than with existing turbines.
The turbine has a hub height of 300 meters (984 feet), and its rotor blades bring its total height to 365 meters. That makes it taller than the Eiffel Tower in Paris, at 330 meters (1,083 feet), and leaves it just short of Berlin's television tower, Germany 's tallest building at 368 meters (1,207 feet).

articles.jina_text:
One of the largest data centers on the East Coast, DataOne is the first in New Jersey seeking to build its own power plant. Photograph: Evan Simon / Floodlight
View image in fullscreen
One of the largest data centers on the East Coast, DataOne is the first in New Jersey seeking to build its own power plant. Photograph: Evan Simon / Floodlight


US datacenter discharged large amounts of pollution for almost a year with no permits


Records show Vineland facility in New Jersey emitted health-harming pollution before regulators stepped in




DataOne, the Microsoft-linked New Jersey datacenter recently hit with a $1m fine for running unpermitted generators, emitted large amounts of health-harming air pollution for nearly a year before state regulators stepped in, according to public records obtained by Floodlight.
The Vineland facility’s 62 gas-fired generators became public in August after a Floodlight/Guardian visual investigation found them operating without permits. The New Jersey department of environmental protection last week fined the company over the fleet but did not disclose how long the generators had been operating nor how much air pollution they had released into the surrounding community over the past year.

Floodlight sent technical data about the generators – obtained through public records requests – to a Rutgers professor and a former EPA air division chief.
“Our best estimate is that the generators emitted about 140 tons of NOx,” said Xiaomeng Jin, an assistant professor at Rutgers department of environmental sciences. Her analysis would rank DataOne in the state’s top five NOx polluters of 2025, per EPA data.
NOx are a dangerous group of smog-producing gases linked to asthma, heart attacks and even premature death. It’s “the most important air pollutant in the US that affects most people”, Jin said.
Longtime Vineland resident Tiffany Leone-Vespa lives about a mile from the data center and said the noise from the generators sounds like an airplane in the back of her house.
“What health problems might I face in the future? Because I’ve been exposed to all of that. My kids have been exposed to it,” she said.
The site’s potential NOx emissions are even larger, according to Jin and Bruce Buckheit – a former EPA air enforcement division chief. Both concluded that at full use, DataOne’s fleet could emit more than 1,500 tons of NOx per year. That is nearly twice the amount that the Linden Cogeneration gas-fired power plant, New Jersey’s largest NOx emitter, is allowed to emit.
Operating the generators “results in very high levels of air pollution” and the fleet’s potential emissions are “well over the regulatory threshold for a new major source”, said Buckheit.
New Jersey labels any facility capable of emitting more than 25 tons of NOx per year a “major source”. Obtaining a major source permit requires extensive environmental reviews, best available pollution controls and public comment periods – all before construction can even begin.

Gavin Newsom says Trump is a ‘gift’ to the climate cause for dispelling notions of fossil fuel energy security




Of all the epithets hurled at Donald Trump since he became US president, perhaps the most unusual was delivered last week – that he is, in fact, some sort of environmentalist.
Trump is the “greatest gift” to the environmental movement, argued Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, due to the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.

“He’s woken the world up to how vulnerable we are to petro-dictatorships, how vulnerable we are to disruptions in the Middle East,” Newsom told the Guardian during Climate Week in New York. “This war has completely gutted any sort of romantic notions of energy security and it’s compelled folks to think differently. It’s accelerating investments and clean energy and renewables.”


If Trump has been an accidental environmentalist, it’s been in the international sphere. The strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of the world’s oil and gas exports usually flow, is now starting to open up but has been routinely snarled since the Iran war began in February, causing the cost of these fossil fuels to soar around the world.
Countries reacted by scrambling to cut their oil and gas use while turning to cleaner forms of energy such as solar and wind (although there’s also been a small uptick in coal, the dirtiest of fossil fuels).
The overall consequence has been a positive one for our shared climate, with global fossil fuel emissions set to drop by 0.5% this year due to the crisis, Carbon Brief has estimated. The peak in oil consumption may have been sped up enough to arrive this year, rather than the previous estimate of 2029, according to the International Energy Agency.



By launching the war, Trump is set to achieve something only dreamed about by climate advocates and not seen outside global economic crashes or the Covid-19 pandemic – an annual reduction in the emissions that are overheating our planet. The president’s imposition of tariffs and importation of foreign ground beef, meanwhile, may also end up hurting the US cattle industry, another major source of greenhouse gas emissions.
“It’s a curious thing to say, but I believe it,” Newsom, a potential contender for the Democratic presidential nomination, said of Trump as a sort of unintentional biophile. “This moment will mark how we can’t go back to our original form.”

The last “super” El Niño to hit London a decade ago brought devastating storms and freezing weather, with experts fearing this winter’s will bring even worse.




The “Godzilla” El Niño expected to hit London this winter could be one of the worst on record, according to experts.








Storm Desmond killed three people and destroyed over 5,000 homes during the winter of 2015/16, the last time there was an El Niño of similar magnitude affecting the UK.




However, the Met Office has said that the El Niño event developing in the tropical Pacific has already “surpassed the magnitude of previous events including the one in 2015/16”.




The national forecaster is predicting a stormier start than usual to autumn and winter, and colder spells at the end of winter.


How have previous ‘El Niño’ events impacted London?




London has been battered by El Niños in a number of previous winters, most significantly in 2015 and 2016.











The event brought Storm Desmond to the UK in early December, with severe gales and record-breaking rainfall hitting much of the country.


Rescue teams evacuate people from their homes after Storm Desmond caused flooding in Carlisle

Though the worst affected areas by Storm Desmond were in northern England, Scotland, and Wales, the capital also felt the force of the storm’s severe winds.







A 90-year-old man died near Finchley Central station in north London, when a gust of wind apparently blew him into the side of a moving bus, according to a Met spokesperson at the time.




The high winds were also blamed for the 60ft Trafalgar Square Christmas Tree leaning at a noticeable angle.

articles.jina_text:
Swiss glaciers shrank by 5.5% in the first eight months of 2026, according to an annual monitoring report, after a summer of scorching heatwaves that followed a winter with little snow. The reduction in ice volume falls just shy of the record set in 2022 and brings the total loss of glacier ice since 2021 to 19.4%.



View image in fullscreen
Glaciologist Matthias Huss records changes in the Scex Rouge glacier above Les Diablerets, western Switzerland. Photograph: Fabrice Coffrini/AFP/Getty
Matthias Huss, a glaciologist at ETH Zürich and lead author of the report, said many people do not realise how fast glaciers are retreating, or that just one generation ago some now-barren sites used to sit beneath hundreds of metres of ice. The scientists have not yet compiled a formal tally of lost glaciers this year but said they had witnessed the death of a number of small ones.
“I visited one last week and it’s so impressive to stand in this moonlike landscape where there was a big layer of ice – an extensive glacier – just a few years ago,” said Huss. “And now it’s a rock desert where there’s some scattered blocks of old ice still lying around and melting on the hot rocks.”
The report, a collaboration between the Swiss Glacier Monitoring Network and the Swiss Commission for Cryosphere Observation, found the mean thickness of individual glaciers fell by between 2.5 metres and 4 metres in 2026. Huss said scientists were increasingly seeing glaciers collapse from the inside – the result of internal streams beneath the ice that excavate caverns – rather than simply retreating from surface heat.



“You have huge holes like cheese in the middle of the ice that have collapsing roofs,” said Huss. “These are processes that tear the glaciers apart and make them retreat even faster.”
Europe is warming twice as fast as the global average from the heat-trapping effects of fossil fuel pollution and the destruction of nature, with Alpine regions experiencing some of the most dramatic changes.


View image in fullscreen
Matthias Huss looks at the ice on the Rhône glacier in Obergoms, Switzerland. Photograph: Pierre Albouy/Reuters
Analysis published by MeteoSwiss on Tuesday found the summer half-year from April to September was the hottest and driest it had been since records began in 1864. In that time, humanity has filled the atmosphere with 1.8tn tons of carbon dioxide and heated the planet by about 1.4C.

The scientists attributed this to limited deposits of Saharan dust, which foul the snow and prevent it from reflecting sunlight, as well as slightly greater snow cover at the end of winter and more sunlight in the summer.

The green light for the largest coalmine in NSW history is shocking proof that our governance systems are betraying Australians

Georgina Woods





There is no greater treachery than this failure to face up to the climate crisis. How can we now fend off despair?





The Independent Planning Commission’s published reasons for approving the largest coalmine in New South Wales history in the context of mounting death, disaster and despair brought on by global heating reads like a hostage statement.
In its decision, the commission accepts that the extension of the Hunter Valley Operations’ mine for a further 19 years – resulting 809m tonnes of greenhouse gas pollution – will materially worsen global warming. The panel members cite CSIRO’s finding that climate change is having a growing effect on the lives and livelihoods of all Australians and that the severity of that impact “will depend on the speed at which global greenhouse gas emissions can be reduced”. They reject the idea that keeping HVO’s coal in the ground would make no difference to global warming.



Despite all of this, the commission has still found that all of this is “outweighed” by the revenues coalmining makes, its centrality to the Hunter’s regional economy and the livelihoods of 1,500 people.
The commission’s jarring and contradictory statement must be read for what it is: an admission that Australia’s governance systems are failing to meet the crisis of climate change. It is a shocking and unsettling admission because our faith in these systems has been the foundation of advocacy for action on the climate emergency for decades.







Approval of biggest coal project in NSW planning commission’s history described as ‘infamous betrayal’

Read more
We vote, we make submissions, we go to court, we meet our MPs, we compile and present evidence. All of this activity rests on a belief in the systems of government that have now clearly failed to meet their solemn public duty. We must seriously consider what avenue remains available to us to fend off despair.
The commission heard direct, heart-rending testimony from people who are already grappling with the damage and loss brought by the climate crisis, from grandparents in anguish about the lives awaiting the little children they love, from scientists patiently outlining devastating evidence about the mine’s climate change impacts. ‘The toll is huge’: El Niño-driven wildfires overwhelm Indonesia’s orangutan population


The global climate phenomenon has triggered devastating infernos in the ape’s Indonesian heartlands, with long-term effects on the animals still unknown




The mother’s hands were peeling from walking on the torched ground. Her eight-month-old baby, which clung to her side, was dehydrated and thin. The pair, named Mama Abu and Abu (“ash” in Indonesian), were found in an oil palm subsidiary estate, rescuers say.
The orangutan pair were saved last month from wildfires that are devouring Indonesia’s forests and peatland, unleashing thick smog, and destroying the habitat of some of the planet’s most vulnerable species.

Primate specialists from the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) have called for urgent international assistance to help control the fires, warning this week that thousands of orangutans could be killed, injured or displaced.
Wildfires happen every year in Indonesia, where fire is often used to clear land to make way for palm or pulp plantations. But the arrival of a supercharged El Niño has brought especially dry conditions, causing blazes to spread rapidly across parts of Sumatra, Kalimantan (the Indonesian part of Borneo) and Papua.
The fires have also taken hold across peatland, which is extremely hard to extinguish as it smoulders underground. In its natural state, it should be waterlogged, but over recent decades, vast areas have been drained by industrial agriculture, leaving it highly flammable.
Habitat containing 52% of the total Bornean orangutan population is now affected by the fires, according to a statement from the IUCN’s primate specialists.
They are not the only animals affected, however. Blazes have also spread into the habitats of five gibbon species, all of which are listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List. Geopix, an environmental NGO, warned earlier this month that 4,500 fires had been detected across 21 Sumatran elephant habitats over recent months.


View image in fullscreen
A fire burning on peatland and forest in Sungai Putri village, West Kalimantan, Indonesia, in August. Photograph: Garry Lotulung/The Guardian
“I believe that the toll on wild animals being burned, dead, because of the fires is huge,” says Dr Karmele Llano Sanchez, a veterinarian and co-founder and CEO of Yiari, a non-profit focused on primate and habitat conservation, which rescues orangutans and other species from torched forests

articles.raw_rss: Scientists say such rapid melting is no longer surprising given the pace of climate change.
articles.raw_meta: Scientists say such rapid melting is no longer surprising given the pace of climate change.
articles.jina_text:
Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.
More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".
They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.
The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.
There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed. 
But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.
The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting. 
Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.














"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.



Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.
And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June, exposing the glacier ice below.
Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy. 
That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.
"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.
"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressing… but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.







Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions. 
Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.
Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply. 
The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.
"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.
"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."

A massive wave of energy is expected to slam into the California coast in October, sending sea levels rising by up to a foot and threatening coastal homes and ecosystems.
The so-called Kelvin wave forms because of sudden changes in wind speed and force, and has the ability to push warm water vast distances for months, according to forecaster AccuWeather.
In this case, the Kelvin wave is driven by strengthening super El Niño conditions, experts say.
The natural climate pattern is forecast to bring more life-threatening flooding rainstorms and extreme temperatures across the U.S. into next year, worsened by human-caused climate change. 





The Kelvin wave is “one of the first, if not the first indication that El Niño is here,” Dillon Amaya, an assistant professor in the department of marine, earth and atmospheric sciences at North Carolina State University, told The New York Times on Wednesday.






open image in gallery
A wave crashes into a seawall protecting beachfront homes on Monday in Long Beach, California. A massive wave of energy is expected to send Pacific sea levels rising along the coast (Getty)
Past El Niño events have raised West Coast water levels by more than 7.9 inches, according to NASA. 
Unfortunately for Californians, that’s not the only reason water levels are expected to swell, too.
The Golden State’s king tides - especially high tides that occur due to the position of the Earth, moon and sun - are expected to be worse than typical this year due to the moon’s location in relation to Earth’s equator. 


Those happen around Thanksgiving and Christmas, Anthony Edwards, a meteorologist at The San Francisco Chronicle, wrote on Monday.
And climate change has brought sea levels inching upward for decades, rising 8-9 inches worldwide since 1880, according to federal data. 



In the now-hurricane-riddled Pacific, sea levels have risen 4-6 inches since 1993, according to the United Nations.





open image in gallery
A jogger makes his way along a flooded Mill Valley bike path during a king tide event in January 2022. This year, the king tides are expected to be even worse than normal (AFP via Getty Images)
These effects have made for some records already in California. The Bay Area got its second-ever coastal flood advisory this month and a previous Kelvin wave caused San Francisco’s highest June and July tides on record.





That’s also part of what led Gov. Gavin Newsom to declare a state of emergency, mobilizing state agencies to distribute sandbags and pumps.

articles.title: Michael Sheen campaign on toxic waste sites wins Senedd backing

articles.jina_text:
Member of the Senedd from all parties have urged Welsh ministers to work with the UK government to make sure polluters pay for cleaning up contaminated land.
A motion introduced by Plaid Cymru MS Niamh Salkeld, backed across party lines, also calls for a UK fund to investigate and remediate sites where costs cannot be recovered, and for a framework to test affected land.
The calls come after a BBC documentary by Michael Sheen examined claims toxic waste poisoned people at 14 sites in Wales and England.
A Welsh government minister promised a plan to "progressively restore post-industrial land" and protect communities from "potential risks".
Earlier this month, Sheen went to Westminster to urge MPs to support a testing programme.



Buried with Michael Sheen

What is the truth lying beneath our feet? Michael Sheen uncovers claims of conspiracy, complicity and denial over alleged toxic 'forever chemical' contamination in south Wales.
Watch on iPlayer




In the Senedd on Thursday, one member after another recounted in detail the history of sites in their area that they were worried about.
Salkeld, who represents the constituency of Blaenau Gwent Caerffili Rhymni, said her motion was about "making sure that the legacy of our industrial past is managed properly and fairly". 
"It's about having a clearer national picture of contaminated land," she said.
"It's about prioritising the sites where the risks are greatest. 
"It's about giving local authorities the support that they need, and it's about making sure that where possible, those responsible for pollution contribute to the cost of putting it right. 
"The communities living alongside these sites did not create this contamination, so they should not be left with carrying the uncertainty, the potential risks, all the costs."

"They deserve a system capable of establishing the facts, and where action is needed, they deserve to know that the money and the determination are there to see it through. 
"As their representatives, the least we can do is to make sure their questions are heard and keep asking them until they get a proper answer."

New UK gas and oil projects are a ‘no-brainer’, says EDF boss


Developing North Sea fields does not contradict net zero goals, according to Simone Rossi




New oil and gas projects are a “no-brainer” that pose “no contradiction” to the net zero agenda, according to the head of EDF Energy.
Simone Rossi has joined a string of renewables leaders in making the case for more North Sea production as the government prepares to decide on two projects there.

He said ministers should give the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields the green light, while accelerating support for heat pumps and electric vehicles.
“It will take decades to wean off from that dependency,” Rossi said in an interview with the BBC. “So while this is happening we should use the resources that we’ve got rather than importing them from afar. For me, it’s really a no-brainer. It is not in contradiction.”


View image in fullscreen
Simone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF Energy, says UK oil and gas projects have lower emissions than imports. Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.
New North Sea developments would help to create jobs and increase government tax receipts that could be used to support households struggling to pay energy bills, according to Rossi.


He said locally produced fossil fuels had lower emissions than imports because they do not need to transported over long distances.
“In the UK the only way we can reduce emissions is to genuinely reduce the usage of fossil fuels at the point of use,” he said. “Over time, the only solution is electricity.”
The boss of EDF Energy, which generates about a fifth of the UK’s low-carbon electricity, has become the latest high-profile advocate of climate action to also make a case for more North Sea production. Others include: Greg Jackson, the founder of Octopus Energy; Jürgen Maier, the former boss of GB Energy; and Tara Singh, the boss of RenewableUK.
EDF Energy, which is owned by EDF of France, has about 8 gigawatts of low-carbon generation capacity in the UK, including eight nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of 6GW and 2GW of wind, solar and battery storage. It is building the much-delayed Hinkley Point C nuclear power station in Somerset.
Politicians to have spoken out in favour of more North Sea production include: the former chancellor Rachel Reeves; the defence secretary, Wes Streeting; former Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar; Liberal Democrat leader and former energy secretary, Ed Davey; and the leaders of the largest trade unions.

Two million people in England unaware their properties are at risk of flooding


Environment Agency warns residents of 6m at-risk properties to prepare for wet and windy three months ahead




More than two million people in England are unaware their properties are at risk of flooding, as the UK braces for a wet and stormy start to the winter, according to the Environment Agency.
Experts say the next three months are more likely than usual to be wet and windy – due to a combination of large-scale weather patterns and the “subtle” impact of a supercharged El Niño – increasing the risk of flooding.

However, the EA warned on Wednesday that people in a third of the six million properties most at risk of flooding are unaware of the threat they face.
Caroline Douglass, the director for flood and coastal risk management at the Environment Agency, said: “We know with the 6m properties at risk [in England] … we know that one-third of people who are at risk don’t think they are at risk.”
She urged people to check on the government website whether their properties were at risk, and to take measures to prepare.
“We want the public to make sure they know what their risk is, so check on gov.uk. We need them to sign up for flood warnings … and if they are at risk, to have a flood plan so they know what they need to do.”

after newsletter promotion







One in nine new homes in England built in areas of flood risk, study shows

Read more
Flooding caused havoc across the UK last year and the Met Office said that, after a summer of droughts, extreme heat and wildfires, the UK was facing a wet and stormy start to winter.
Will Lang, the chief meteorologist with the Met Office, said its three-month outlook indicated there was an increased likelihood that October, November and December would be wet and windy, adding there were early indications of drier, colder and calmer conditions later in the winter.
“There is an increasing likelihood of it being wet overall, windier than normal and milder than usual as well,” said Lang.
He said El Niño – which is bringing devastation to other parts of the world – increased the likelihood of wetter and windier conditions in the UK but was only one of several factors influencing the UK’s weather. “This is just a subtle shift in the odds of it being wetter and windier,” he said. But he added that would lead to “a heightened potential for flooding”.

Urgewald tracked loans and underwriting from 744 commercial banks around the world to companies operating across the ‘coal value chain’. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP
View image in fullscreen
Urgewald tracked loans and underwriting from 744 commercial banks around the world to companies operating across the ‘coal value chain’. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP


UK banks are Europe’s biggest coal financiers, report finds


Study says UK-based banks provided $8.3bn in coal financing in four years, with Barclays and HSBC leading rise




UK banks are Europe’s biggest financial backers of the global coal industry, providing billions of pounds in funding for the climate-wrecking fossil fuel in the past four years, according to a report.
The study found UK-based banks had provided $8.3bn (£6.2bn) in coal financing since Cop26 in Glasgow in 2021, when global leaders pledged to “phase down” coal use. This compared with $4.9bn from German banks and $3.4bn from French banks over the same period.

The sums provided by UK banks were largely driven by Barclays and HSBC, which both increased their coal financing between 2022 and 2025 despite high-profile climate and net zero commitments, according to the research.
It found Barclays’ coal financing increased by 34%, from approximately $1.2bn in 2022 to $1.6bn in 2025, while HSBC’s more than doubled from $200m to $414m.
The research was carried out by Urgewald, a Germany-based environmental and human rights organisation. It tracked loans and underwriting from 744 commercial banks around the world to companies operating across the “coal value chain” – those organisations involved in every aspect of the industry, from mines and power generation to logistics, exploration and trading organisations.
Heffa Schücking, the director of Urgewald, said: “Barclays and HSBC should explain why their financing is moving in the opposite direction to the rest of Europe.”
A spokesperson for HSBC said the bank had committed to phasing out financing “for thermal coal-fired power and thermal coal mining” by 2030 in EU and OECD markets and by 2040 in other markets.
They added: “These commitments support our ambition to align the financed emissions in our portfolio with net zero by 2050. As reported in our 2025 annual report and accounts, financed emissions from thermal coal mining fell by 94% between 2020 and 2024, while reported thermal coal financing exposures, calculated on the basis set out in our disclosures, fell from approximately $1bn to approximately $0.5bn over the same period.”
A spokesperson for Barclays said many of the companies named in the report were “diversified energy or mining companies”. They said Barclays did not provide financing to companies that generated “more than 30% of revenues from thermal coal mining or power generation”.

India's foreign minister S Jaishankar has warned that the world faces a "major food crisis" in the coming months, as wars in Ukraine and the Middle East compound the effects of a super El Nino.
Speaking at an event organised by the Asia Society in New York, Mr Jaishankar said the two conflicts had "a devastating impact" on the economies of the Global South, and that energy, food, fertiliser and finance were all under strain at once.
"If you have energy as a big crunch and then food and fertilisers on top of it, and finance, because every time there's a conflict, money moves towards safe harbours and away from the Global South, the net result of it has been really very, very stressful," he said.





Mr Jaishankar said tight global energy markets were being worsened by countries "playing politics" with oil supplies, driving up prices at a time when they should be stabilising. 
"Part of it is actually the security of oil supplies and part of it is the politics of oil supplies, and they are feeding into each other and creating an aggravated crisis," he said.

articles.jina_text:
Homes in Long Beach, California, in a waning swell from Hurricane Marie, on 8 September. Photograph: Kelvin Kuo/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Homes in Long Beach, California, in a waning swell from Hurricane Marie, on 8 September. Photograph: Kelvin Kuo/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images


California rushes to prepare for massive ‘Kelvin’ wave and predicted sea level rise 


Wave nearing southern California expected to reach San Francisco Bay Area by October as it crawls toward Alaska




Communities across California are rushing to prepare for the imminent arrival of the so-called “Kelvin wave”, a massive underwater band of warm water threatening to inundate swaths of the vast North American shoreline.
The wave is nearing southern California and expected to reach the San Francisco Bay Area by early October, as it crawls toward Alaska. Waters could rise by a foot along the California coast, according to scientists, who have warned that this could dramatically double the 8-12in rise in sea levels already caused by climate change over the last century.








Concern mounts over slow-moving, planetary-scale ‘Kelvin’ wave heading for California

Read more
The Kelvin wave doesn’t climb and crash like a typical ocean wave; rather, it swells the tides from beneath the surface. It’s effectively a massive slosh of warm water, driven by El Niño conditions, that moves across the Pacific before colliding with the South American coastline and surging north. It also won’t transport water in the way a tsunami might, but creates conditions that enable higher sea levels to linger.
On their own, Kelvin waves aren’t always hazardous, according to Mike Jacox, a research oceanographer with the National Marine Fisheries Service, though they can reduce the growth of phytoplankton that form the base of the marine food web. “But when there are very high tides or storm surges, their effects can be amplified,” he said.


If the rising waters coincide with other climatic events, such as rainstorms and high tides, the phenomenon could swallow beaches, chew away bluffs and coastlines, and submerge streets, homes and businesses.


“This coming Kelvin wave is just the beginning,” said Dr Jonathan Warrick, a research geologist at the US Geological Survey. “The thing to look out for is what will happen in January, February and March – that’s when we get the biggest storms, we get our largest waves and we have some very large tides.”
If these events align, their effects will compound, setting the stage for a tumultuous winter. Together, Warrick said, the systems will pack a far bigger punch. “When it comes to these storms and the tides,” he said, “we really are kind of rolling the dice.”

articles.raw_rss: Insects provide protection, sanitation and even shelter to vertebrates, making them a priority for conservation effortsFor many vertebrates, insects are more than a food source. articles.raw_meta: Insects provide protection, sanitation and even shelter to vertebrates, making them a priority for conservation efforts
articles.jina_text:
For many vertebrates, insects are more than a food source. As “little things that run the world”, insects provide critical functions such as protection, sanitation and shelter across ecosystems, according to a new study.
The study, published in Nature Reviews Biodiversity on Wednesday, sheds light on the various ways insects support vertebrates, ranging from birds and bats to reptiles, amphibians and mammals.

Nearly three-quarters of terrestrial and freshwater vertebrates eat invertebrates, according to the paper, with insects frequently making up a large portion of their diets.
However, their relationship goes beyond predator and prey.







Scientists are fighting a longer mosquito season with ... more mosquitoes

Read more
The paper, led by Eliza Grames, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Binghamton University, State University of New York, documents dozens of less obvious ways vertebrates depend on the estimated 14m to 30m species of insects found around the world.
Chimpanzees, for example, have been recorded applying insects to treat open wounds, while more than 200 bird species use ants to remove parasites or maintain feathers. Other birds build nests near wasps or other stinging insects, in a likely effort to gain protection from predators.
Insects also provide shelter, the study notes. Birds, reptiles and mammals use termite mounds and ant nests, which can offer stable temperatures and humidity. White-throated round-eared bats, for instance, excavate cavities in termite mounds and use them as roosts.


Other insects act as sanitation workers. Dung beetles remove animal waste and can make dung drier and more aerated, in turn reducing parasite survival, according to the study. Meanwhile, moths living in some bird nests consume feces, feathers and other debris. The review notes that insects have performed similar functions for millions of years, citing evidence of beetles feeding on feathers in dinosaur nests during the Cretaceous period, which lasted from around 145m to 66m years ago.
Other insect-vertebrate relationships include beetles removing ectoparasites from rodents and snakes feeding on firefly larvae to obtain defensive toxins, as well as antbirds using live crickets during courtship.
Mutually beneficial relationships also occur across the insect-vertebrate realm, with sloths relying on moths to deposit nitrogen in their fur and spur algal growth, which the sloths then eat. Sloths then descend from trees once a month to defecate on the ground, providing substrate in which moths lay eggs.
According to the study, such overlooked relationships could become increasingly important as insect communities evolve. Although the extent of insect declines varies across habitats and regions, the review says that “widespread and considerable disruption” of insect communities is “inevitable” as land use changes.


Grames called the study a “wake-up call for anyone concerned about the biodiversity crisis”.

articles.title: Young minds develop ideas to tackle climate change
articles.raw_rss: Sixteen teenagers take part in a hackathon to devise ways to combat issues such as light pollution.
articles.raw_meta: Sixteen teenagers take part in a hackathon to devise ways to combat issues such as light pollution.
articles.jina_text:
A group of young people have developed ideas to tackle the effects of climate change as part of a free touring exhibition.
On Tuesday 16 young people took part in a hackathon - a timed event where people work together to build creative solutions to problems - where they devised posters with ways to combat light pollution, wild fires, damage to oceans and poor water quality.
The event was hosted by Seeds of Hope and Change, an organisation run by the Soka Gakkai International and the UN Earth Charter, at the Jerwood Dancehouse in Ipswich.
Maryanne, 16, took part in the project and said: "We just want people to be aware of what's going on, especially with major issues such as ocean pollution."




Image source, Jon Wright/BBC
Image caption, 

Maryanne and Hannah discussed the challenge of pollution in seas and oceans




Climate change is the long-term shift in the Earth's average temperatures and weather conditions.
This year's summer was the UK's hottest on record, according to provisional data from the Met Office.
The Met Office said the heat experienced this summer was made about 130 times more likely by human-induced climate change. 
Baveen, 17, said "We wanted to talk about the cities and the sky and how it affects people and also wildlife."
The poster her group produced included ideas for using low-intensity bulbs and motion sensors in street lights so that they were not continuously left on.




Image source, Jon Wright/BBC
Image caption, 

Each group at the hackathon put their ideas on big posters




The exhibition, which is free and runs until 4 October, includes 24 pop-up panels that share information and environmental case studies from around the world on the impact of climate change. 
The hackathon for young people was run by ambassadors from the youth-led campaigning organisation #iWill.
Alex Harrison, one of the #iWill ambassadors, said: "The main purpose is reminding young people that in the face of something really scary like climate change, there's a lot that you can do personally to make a real change."




Image source, Jon Wright/BBC
Image caption, 

The exhibition of 24 pop-up panels share information and environmental case studies from around the world

The PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deed





As Andy Burnham delivered his conference speech to the Labour faithful yesterday, it was hard not to recall Jeremy Corbyn’s words after the party’s shattering 2019 election defeat. “I am proud that on austerity, on corporate power, on inequality and the climate emergency,” he wrote for this publication, “we have won the arguments and rewritten the terms of political debate.” Given Boris Johnson’s 80-seat majority, widespread mockery ensued.
But when it comes to rhetoric, who can now deny that the left has won the argument? A Labour prime minister has declared that “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time”, listing five villains: “Deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity, Brexit.” His speech was infused with class politics, as he condemned a society “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”.



When he committed to break with the “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”, he lumped together Conservative and Labour governments. He has already repeatedly labelled the culprit: neoliberalism. This has long been the received wisdom of the left: that as Clement Attlee’s postwar government established a social-democratic consensus that the Tories upheld for a generation, so Margaret Thatcher bequeathed a settlement that New Labour maintained.

Bleached coral in Thailand: Between January 2023 and September 2025, 84% of global coral reefs experienced bleaching-level heat stress. Photograph: Napat Wesshasartar/Reuters
View image in fullscreen
Bleached coral in Thailand: Between January 2023 and September 2025, 84% of global coral reefs experienced bleaching-level heat stress. Photograph: Napat Wesshasartar/Reuters


World’s oceans absorbed record heat equal to 40 times annual global energy use


The injection of thermal energy comes amid an increasing rise in sea levels and continuing acidification




A record-breaking 23 zettajoules of heat was sunk into the world’s seas last year, leaving ocean waters hotter, higher and less hospitable, a report has found.
The explosive addition of thermal energy, which was almost 40 times greater than all the energy humanity used that year, comes amid far-reaching changes to the deep water bodies fundamental to life on Earth.

Sea levels have risen by about 3.8mm per year since 1999, and at a faster rate of 4.2mm per year between 2012 and 2025, according to the 10th edition of the Copernicus ocean state report. It found the global ocean has become 17% more acidic in the last 40 years.







What are zettajoules – and what do they tell us about Earth’s energy imbalance?

Read more
Oceans have absorbed about one-third of the carbon dioxide that humanity has spewed and about 90% of the extra heat that greenhouse gas pollution has trapped in the Earth’s system.
“The ocean is transforming before our eyes,” said Pierre Bahurel, director general of Mercator Ocean International, which published the report. “Warming, rising seas and ecosystem degradation are interconnected signs of significant and long-term change.”
In Europe, which is heating twice as fast as the global average, the Mediterranean and Black Seas have been plagued by record-breaking marine heatwaves – with elevated temperatures that persist deep below the surface – and bouts of extreme heat that have lasted more than a month, the scientists found.


View image in fullscreen
A Mediterranean swimmer in mid-January: the entire sea has warmed by .32C per decade. Photograph: Hassan Ammar/AP
The scientists found a clear acceleration of sea level rise in the western Mediterranean, even as the eastern part showed uneven gains. The entire sea has warmed by 0.32C per decade, the report found, driving up marine heatwaves, particularly in the last few years. A joule, the unit used to measure heat, is the amount of electricity required to run a one watt device for one second; a zettajoule is a billion trillion joules.


The report comes as western Europe experiences an unusually warm September right after its ruinously fiery summer, with temperatures hitting 40C highs in parts of Spain and Portugal last week. Hot coastal waters exacerbate heatwaves on land by adding heat during nights that would otherwise cool down.

The New South Wales independent planner has approved the biggest coalmine project to ever go before it, allowing mining to continue until 2045 at a Hunter Valley project described by climate groups as a “carbon bomb”.
The Independent Planning Commission (IPC) has greenlit the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) Continuation Project after a contentious assessment that drew in climate and environment groups, unions, state authorities and more than 10,000 public submissions.

On Wednesday, the commission said the greenhouse gas emissions from the mine, near Singleton, would “contribute to climate change impacts on the people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”.







Locals fear for their children’s quality of life if the biggest coalmine extension in NSW is approved 

Read more
But these impacts had been “outweighed by its benefits to the Hunter region and NSW, including continued employment, economic activity, support for local business, ongoing royalties and taxation revenue”.
The IPC said the decision would “provide economic stability for the Hunter region and support a more orderly transition for workers, businesses and communities as the coal industry changes over time”.
In response, Georgina Woods, the co-national coordinator of the Lock the Gate Alliance, said: “There is no other way to describe this other than a catastrophic failure of the New South Wales planning system to protect the people of the state from the worst impacts of global warming.”
Climate campaigners had strongly opposed the project, saying it was out of line with Australia’s commitments under the Paris climate agreement and could affect extreme weather events.

An EV sold every 100 seconds: Australian demand for electric cars more than doubles


A record 157,957 new EVs were sold nationally between January and June, according to the Electric Vehicle Council 
 
 
Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates 
 
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast 




Australians are buying electric vehicles at record levels, with sales more than doubling year on year and occurring at a rate equivalent to one EV sold every 100 seconds.
A record 157,957 EV sales occurred between January and June – an 117% increase on the same period last year, according to a new report released by the Electric Vehicle Council.

Comparatively, petrol and diesel vehicle sales decreased by 14% year on year, according to the council’s chief executive, Julie Delvecchio.

Read more
EVs accounted for one in four new vehicles sold in the first half of the year, up 12.1% from the first six months of 2025, the state of EVs report said.
“EVs are being taken up as a cost-of-living measure by households across Australia,” Delvecchio said of the rise, noting that the ongoing fuel crisis was an accelerating factor but was “not the starting gun”.
“It exposed the value of the policy work that had already been done – and made the lower running costs and energy security benefits of EVs much more immediate for Australian households,” she said.


The new figures include about 104,000 battery electric vehicles and 54,000 plug-in hybrids.
As of June, there were 612,000 EVs in the national vehicle fleet. “We are well on track to hit the target of 1 million EVs on Australian roads by next year,” said Aman Gaur, the head of policy and advocacy at the EV Council.
The Australian Capital Territory, where 44% of new cars registered are electric, retained its crown as the nation’s EV capital.
Tarneit, in Melbourne’s west, was the individual postcode with the highest uptake.
A key driver of the growing uptake has been the national vehicle efficiency standard, which requires carmakers to supply new vehicles that meet an average per-kilometre emissions target.
The standard had “substantially increased the options and the price competitiveness of EVs”, with nearly 200 EV models available in 2026, Gaur said.
The council is pushing for the federal government to extend the standard beyond 2029, to align with the government’s 2035 emissions reduction target.

articles.summary: Australian electric vehicle sales have more than doubled year on year, with a record 157,957 EVs sold in the first half of the year — equivalent to one sale every 100 seconds. EVs now account for one in four new vehicles sold, while petrol and diesel vehicle sales fell by 14% over the same period. Experts say EVs are increasingly being adopted as a cost-of-living measure, with the ongoing fuel crisis accelerating but not initiating the trend.
